true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate `self.downsize` definition silently discards the original 4-arg method

The pre-existing method `def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` (lines 145-147) is immediately redefined by a new `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` (lines 149-151). In Ruby, the second definition silently replaces the first in the method table (producing a 'method redefined' warning), so any existing caller that invokes `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, max_width, max_height, opts)` with separate width/height arguments (e.g. thumbnail-creation code elsewhere in the app that previously relied on this 4-positional-argument signature) will now raise `ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments` at runtime, because the surviving method only accepts 3 positional arguments plus an options hash. This breaks any existing thumbnail/downsize call site that isn't in this diff, not just the new feature path.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side max upload size hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring configured site settings

`validateUploadedFile` previously read `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, honoring separate admin-configured limits for images (`max_image_size_kb`) and attachments (`max_attachment_size_kb`). It is now hardcoded to `10 * 1024` KB for both types. Attachments cannot be downsized server-side the way images can, so an admin who configured a smaller `max_attachment_size_kb` will no longer have that limit enforced client-side; uploads up to 10MB will be attempted and only fail (if at all) after the fact, producing a confusing UX and bypassing the admin's intended restriction. The same hardcoding is repeated for the 413 (entity too large) error message at line 246, which previously reported `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` and can now show an incorrect max size to users if the server's actual limit differs from 10MB.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
API URL download size limit hardcoded to 10MB regardless of site settings

`FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, "discourse-upload-#{type}")` replaces the previous `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` limit with a fixed 10MB constant. Since `type` can represent non-image attachments as well as images, this removes any admin-configurable control over how large a file the server will fetch via the API URL path (e.g. `max_attachment_size_kb`), silently allowing downloads up to 10MB even on sites configured with a much smaller limit, and wasting bandwidth/memory for attachments that cannot later be downsized.

Animated GIF detection never triggers because tempfile paths have no extension

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)` passes `tempfile.path` as the `from` argument. Inside `OptimizedImage.optimize`, the check `from =~ /\.GIF$/i` (optimized_image.rb line 155) decides whether to use the gifsicle-based animated instructions. Rack/ActionDispatch tempfiles typically have no file extension (e.g. `/tmp/RackMultipart...`), so this regex will never match for uploads coming through this new code path. As a result, large animated GIFs that need downsizing will always go through the regular ImageMagick `downsize_instructions`, which selects only the first frame (`#{from}[0]`), silently stripping the animation from any animated GIF that exceeds `max_image_size_kb`.

Downsizing loop ignores failure and may silently upload an oversized image

The loop at lines 64-70 calls `OptimizedImage.downsize` up to 5 times but never checks its boolean return value. `convert_with` (and therefore `downsize`) returns `false` on any ImageMagick/gifsicle failure (e.g. missing binary, malformed input, unsupported geometry string). If downsizing fails on every attempt, the loop exits solely because `attempt` reaches 0, and the code proceeds to call `Upload.create_for` with the original oversized `tempfile` and no error is surfaced to the caller or the user. This defeats the purpose of the size check and can let files larger than the configured `max_image_size_kb` through unnoticed.

No test coverage for the new automatic downsizing feature

The PR adds a new downsize-on-upload code path (lines 63-70) plus corresponding API changes in `optimized_image.rb` (collapsing `downsize` to a 3-arg/percent-based signature), but no tests were added or updated to cover: downsizing being triggered when `max_image_size_kb` is exceeded, the loop giving up after 5 attempts, or the behavior change to `OptimizedImage.downsize`'s signature. Given this changes both a public model API and upload behavior, the lack of tests makes it easy for the regressions noted above (duplicate method definition, lost GIF animation, silent oversized uploads) to go unnoticed before release.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation callback raises NoMethodError when host is nil

`self.host.sub!(/^https?:\/\//, '')` and the following line assume `host` is always a String. If `host` is `nil` (e.g. a client sends a create/update request without the `host` param, or a new EmbeddableHost record is saved before the field is populated), this raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'sub!' for nil:NilClass` instead of surfacing a normal validation error, causing a 500 response rather than a controlled 422/validation failure.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
update/destroy actions crash with NoMethodError when id is not found

In both `update` (line 10) and `destroy` (line 15), `EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` can return `nil` if the id doesn't exist (e.g. already deleted, race condition, or a bad id). `destroy` then calls `host.destroy` on `nil`, and `update`'s `save_host(nil)` calls `host.host = ...` on `nil`, both raising `NoMethodError` and resulting in an unhandled 500 error instead of a proper 404/error response.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fabricator file contents swapped between category_fabricator.rb and embeddable_host_fabricator.rb

`spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb` now only defines `Fabricator(:embeddable_host)`, while the newly added `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` contains all the `:category`, `:diff_category`, `:happy_category`, and `:private_category` fabricators. The file names no longer match their contents, which is misleading for anyone maintaining these fabricators later (Fabrication itself doesn't care about filenames, so tests still pass, but this is a clear naming/organization mistake that should be corrected).

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unescaped string interpolation into SQL INSERT in migration

`execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', ...)"` interpolates the raw `host` value (read from the previous `embeddable_hosts` site setting) directly into a SQL string without escaping/quoting. Any host string containing a single quote will break the SQL statement or allow arbitrary SQL to run during migration. It should use `ActiveRecord::Base.connection.quote(h)` or parameterized execution.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when no 'embed_category' site_setting row exists

`execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories AS c INNER JOIN site_settings AS s ON s.value = c.name WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'].to_i` assumes the query returns at least one row. Since `embed_category` was historically a setting that is only persisted in `site_settings` when an admin explicitly changed it from its default, most installations will have zero matching rows, making `execute(...)[0]` return `nil`. Calling `['id']` on `nil` raises `NoMethodError`, which will abort the migration for the common case of a site that never customized `embed_category`. The fallback lookup on the next line (`uncategorized_category_id`) has the same unguarded-indexing problem if that setting was never persisted either.

false_negatives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.

false_positives.candidate:
New admin controllers have no functional test coverage

Both `spec/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller_spec.rb` and `spec/controllers/admin/embedding_controller_spec.rb` only assert that the controller class is a subclass of `Admin::AdminController`. There is no test coverage for `create`, `update`, `destroy`, or `show` actions, including important edge cases such as updating/destroying a non-existent id (which, per the related finding, currently raises an unhandled `NoMethodError`), invalid host formats, or the embedding/`embeddable_hosts` payload shape returned to the client. This leaves the new admin embedding feature essentially untested at the controller level.

String#replace without global flag only replaces the first underscore

`type.replace('_', '-')` uses a plain string argument (not a regex with the `g` flag), so only the first underscore in `type` is replaced. This works for `embeddable_host` (single underscore) but will silently fail to fully convert any future model/type name containing more than one underscore, causing `ADMIN_MODELS.indexOf(...)` to miss a match and route requests to the wrong base path.

expandable_first_post? no longer checks whether any embeddable host is configured

Previously `expandable_first_post?` required `SiteSetting.embeddable_hosts.present?` in addition to `embed_truncate?` and `has_topic_embed?`. The new implementation (`SiteSetting.embed_truncate? && has_topic_embed?`) drops the check for whether any `EmbeddableHost` exists, so the 'expand' affordance for truncated embedded posts can now be shown even when no embeddable host is configured (feature effectively disabled). The accompanying spec in spec/models/topic_spec.rb ("is false if embeddable_host is blank") still passes, but only because `embed_truncate` defaults to false, not because the embeddable-host condition is actually exercised — so this behavior is both a quiet regression and untested.

has_many association missing include: true, embeddable_hosts likely omitted from JSON response

`has_many :embeddable_hosts, serializer: EmbeddableHostSerializer, embed: :ids` only emits an `embeddable_host_ids` array on the `embedding` object; without `include: true` the actual host records are not embedded at the root of the payload. The client-side `store.js` `_hydrateEmbedded` logic for `_id(s?)$` keys expects a sibling root-level `embeddable_hosts` collection to resolve each id against (`root[this.pluralize(subType)]`). Without that sibling collection, hydration will produce an array of `undefined` entries, breaking `embedding.embeddable_hosts` on the client and causing the admin embedding page (table rendering, addHost/deleteHost actions) to fail or render incorrectly.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
unsubscribe action crashes when no TopicUser record exists

In TopicsController#unsubscribe, `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil for any logged-in user who can see the topic but has never had a TopicUser row created for it (e.g. never visited it and never received an email about it, since TopicUser is normally created lazily). The very next line calls `tu.notification_level` with no nil check, which raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'notification_level' for nil`, producing a 500 error for any such request (e.g. someone directly navigating to /t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe for a topic they haven't interacted with).

true_positives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Typo in computed property name 'stopNotificiationsText'

The property is named `stopNotificiationsText` (extra 'i', missing proper spelling of 'Notifications') instead of `stopNotificationsText`. It is referenced consistently with the same typo in app/assets/javascripts/discourse/templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs line 3, so it works, but the misspelling makes the code harder to find/search/maintain and looks unprofessional in a user-facing feature.

false_positives.candidate:
"stop_notifications" message is inaccurate when the user was watching/tracking the topic

The text "You will stop receiving notifications for <title>" is shown unconditionally by the unsubscribe page/controller, but the backend logic in TopicsController#unsubscribe (lines 107-111) only sets notification_level to `muted` when it was already `regular` or below; if the user was `tracking` or `watching`, it is merely downgraded to `regular`, which still generates notifications for mentions/replies. The displayed copy therefore overstates the actual effect for a large class of users (anyone above 'regular'), who will continue to receive some notifications despite being told they will 'stop receiving notifications'.

Direct TopicUser save bypasses the canonical TopicUser.change path

The new action mutates `tu.notification_level` and calls `tu.save!` directly instead of using `TopicUser.change(current_user, topic_id, notification_level: ...)`, which is the method used everywhere else in the codebase (e.g. TopicsController#set_notifications) for this kind of update. This bypasses: setting `notifications_changed_at`/`notifications_reason_id`, publishing the `/topic/#{topic_id}` MessageBus event (so any other open tab/browser showing the topic will not reflect the new notification state in real time), and the `observe_after_save_callbacks_for` hook (e.g. UserActionObserver). This creates an inconsistent code path for notification-level changes and a real-time UI sync gap.

No assertion that the new unsubscribe_url renders in the email body/html_part

The test was updated to pass `unsubscribe_url: "/t/1234/unsubscribe"` to `Email::MessageBuilder.new`, but none of the existing assertions check that this value actually appears in `message_with_unsubscribe.body` or `html_part` output. The only existing assertion still just checks for `user_preferences_url`. This leaves the new per-topic unsubscribe link functionality (the actual feature of this PR) without direct test coverage, and would not catch the `I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument` risk described above if `unsubscribe_url` were ever omitted by a caller.

No controller spec coverage for the new unsubscribe action

The new TopicsController#unsubscribe action introduces non-trivial logic (slug-mismatch redirect, JSON vs HTML handling, toggling notification_level based on current state, and a dependency on an existing TopicUser row) but no corresponding spec file changes are included in this PR (no updates to spec/controllers/topics_controller_spec.rb). Given the nil-TopicUser crash risk and the notification-level toggling logic described above, this feature ships without any automated regression protection.

No test added for new Topic#unsubscribe_url helper

The new `unsubscribe_url` method on Topic (returning `"#{url}/unsubscribe"`) has no accompanying unit test verifying its output format, despite being a new public API used both by the mailer and the controller's redirect logic.

Notification-level mutation performed as a side effect of a plain GET request, with no idempotency or CSRF protection The new `unsubscribe` action (routed via GET in config/routes.rb lines 440-441) mutates `TopicUser#notification_level` directly inside a GET request handler, with no confirmation step and no CSRF protection (GET requests are not covered by Rails' CSRF token checks). Because the action is keyed off the logged-in session (current_user) rather than a signed one-time token (unlike the existing key-based `email/unsubscribe/:key` route), any page that causes the user's browser to issue a GET to this URL while they are logged in (e.g. an tag, link prefetching, or an email security scanner following the link) can silently change their notification settings. Additionally, the mutation is not idempotent: every visit to the same URL re-evaluates `tu.notification_level > regular` using the *current* (already mutated) value, so repeated visits (page refresh, back/forward navigation, duplicate email link clicks, or automated re-fetching) progressively downgrade watching/tracking -> regular -> muted, fully muting the topic after just two visits even though the user only intended a single click.

unsubscribe_link translation now silently requires an unsubscribe_url interpolation value

`config/locales/server.en.yml`'s `unsubscribe_link` key now contains `%{unsubscribe_url}`, which `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` (used in both `html_part` at line 67 and `body` at line 90) will try to interpolate. `template_args` only contains `:unsubscribe_url` if the caller of `build_email`/`MessageBuilder.new` passed it in `opts`. Currently only `send_notification_email` in user_notifications.rb supplies it alongside `add_unsubscribe_link: true`, but this is an implicit, unenforced contract: any other current or future caller that sets `add_unsubscribe_link: true` without also passing `unsubscribe_url` will raise `I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument` at email-build time, breaking that notification email entirely.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BlockedEmail match_count/last_match_at are double-counted per signup attempt

In UsersController#create, `user.valid?` is called explicitly (line 168) and then `user.save` is called again a few lines later (line 172). Rails reruns all validations on every call to valid?/save, so the new EmailValidator (and therefore BlockedEmail.should_block?, which mutates and saves the matched BlockedEmail row) executes twice per request. This means `match_count` is incremented by 2 instead of 1 and `last_match_at`/the extra `BlockedEmail` lookup+save happen twice for every single signup attempt (not just discourse-hub flows, since `user.valid?` is evaluated unconditionally due to `&&` short-circuit order). This corrupts the statistics the feature is meant to produce and doubles the DB load added by this feature on every signup.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive, allowing trivial bypass

`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` performs an exact, case-sensitive string match against the stored email. Since email addresses are effectively case-insensitive, a spammer whose address was blocked (e.g. `spam@example.com`) can bypass the block entirely simply by submitting `Spam@Example.com` or any other casing variant. This defeats the purpose of the feature. The whitelist/blacklist domain check in lib/validators/email_validator.rb uses a case-insensitive regex, but the new block-list lookup does not normalize case at all.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
EmailValidator spec omits whitelist/blacklist coverage removed from User model

The domain whitelist/blacklist validation logic previously lived in User#email_validator/email_in_restriction_setting? and is now moved into EmailValidator (lib/validators/email_validator.rb), but this new spec file only exercises the 'blocked email' branch. There is no test verifying `email_domains_whitelist`/`email_domains_blacklist` behavior still works correctly after being relocated out of user.rb, leaving that previously-tested logic without direct validator-level coverage.

New rejectedEmails client logic has no test coverage

The new rejectedEmails tracking in emailValidation (lines 69-74) and the pushObject call in createAccount (lines 274-276) introduce new client-visible behavior that gates form submission, but no JS unit test was added to verify that a rejected email correctly fails emailValidation/submitDisabled or that successful resubmission with a different email clears the failure.

No end-to-end test for blocked-email signup rejection or new response fields

The create action now returns `errors` and `values` fields on failure specifically to support the new client-side rejectedEmails tracking, and signups are expected to be rejected when the submitted email matches a BlockedEmail record. There is no request/controller spec asserting that POST /users with a blocked email is rejected and that the JSON response includes the `errors`/`values` keys the JS controller depends on. Only the isolated EmailValidator and BlockedEmail model specs exist, so the full integration path (controller -> User#valid? -> EmailValidator -> BlockedEmail) is untested.

Non-atomic read-modify-write race on match_count

should_block? loads the BlockedEmail row, increments `match_count` in Ruby, then calls `save`. Two concurrent signup requests for the same blocked email can both read the same `match_count` value before either writes back, so one increment is silently lost (classic lost-update race). The statistic is also not updated atomically with respect to `last_match_at`. This should use an atomic DB update (e.g. `update_counters`, `increment!`, or a raw SQL `UPDATE ... SET match_count = match_count + 1`) instead of a load-then-save round trip.

rejectedEmails array is a shared mutable default shared across controller instances

`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is declared as a plain property value in `.extend()`, so this exact array object is evaluated once at class-definition time and shared by the prototype. `createAccount` later calls `pushObject` on it (line 275), mutating the shared array in place. Any new instance of CreateAccountController created later (e.g. if the modal controller is re-instantiated) will see emails rejected by a completely unrelated prior session/instance, incorrectly failing emailValidation for emails that were never rejected for that instance. The array should be initialized per-instance in an `init()` hook instead of as a literal default value.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring match instead of exact comparison

`postMessageReceived` validates the message sender with `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1`. This checks whether `e.origin` occurs anywhere inside `discourseUrl` rather than requiring an exact origin match. A malicious page whose origin happens to be a prefix (or other substring) of the configured `discourseUrl` string would pass this check and be able to send fake `discourse-resize` messages (and any future message types added to this handler) to the embedding page. The check should compare `e.origin` against the expected origin with strict equality rather than `indexOf`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Invalid Ruby syntax `end if` breaks the embed view

The template closes the `if/else` block with `<%- end if %>` instead of `<%- end %>`. `end if` with no condition after `if` is not valid Ruby (the `if` keyword here has nothing to modify/condition on), so this template will raise a SyntaxError (wrapped in ActionView::Template::Error) whenever it is compiled/rendered. Since this view is rendered whenever `EmbedController#best` finds an existing `topic_id`, the core feature of this PR (showing embedded discourse comments) will 500 for every successful request. This should simply be `<%- end %>`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feed item content assumed always present; no test for malformed/short items

`content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes every RSS/Atom item exposes a non-nil `content` (e.g. `content:encoded`). Plain RSS 2.0 feeds frequently only provide `description`, in which case `i.content` can be `nil`, causing `nil.scrub` to raise `NoMethodError` and fail the whole scheduled job (no items get imported, not just the bad one). There is no test exercising `poll_feed` itself (spec/jobs/poll_feed_spec.rb only tests the guard conditions in `execute`), so this failure mode is untested and unguarded.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

false_positives.candidate:
Disqus import tool silently drops the --category option

The previous implementation accepted `-c/--category` to assign imported Disqus threads to a specific category and passed `category: category_id` into `PostCreator.new`. The new implementation calls `TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], title: t[:title])`, which has no way to specify a category, and the `method_option :category` declaration itself was removed. Any existing script or documentation relying on `thor disqus:import -c <category>` will now silently ignore the option (or error, since the option no longer exists), a backward-incompatible regression with no migration note.

Race condition can raise unhandled uniqueness violation in TopicEmbed.import

When `embed.blank?` is true, a new Topic/Post/TopicEmbed is created. Two concurrent calls to `import` for the same new `embed_url` (e.g. two users hitting the embed controller at the same time before any embed exists) can both see `embed.blank? == true` and both attempt `TopicEmbed.create!(embed_url: url, ...)`. The unique index on `embed_url` (migration 20131217174004) will reject the second insert, but there is no rescue for `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique`/`StatementInvalid`, so the second caller's `TopicRetriever`/background job will raise an unhandled exception instead of gracefully reusing the already-created embed.

Same cache duration applied to loading and completed states

`discourse_expires_in 1.minute` is called unconditionally for both the "loading" (topic not yet retrieved) and "found" (topic_view rendered) branches. If any HTTP cache/CDN sits in front of this response, the "loading" page can be cached for up to a minute, so the client-side `document.location.reload()` in `loading.html.erb` (which fires every 30s) may keep receiving the stale cached loading page even after the topic has actually been imported, delaying the user from seeing the real content.

Test does not stub TopicView.new's return value

`TopicEmbed.expects(:topic_id_for_embed).returns(123)` and `TopicView.expects(:new).with(123, nil, {best: 5})` mock `TopicView.new` without a `.returns(...)`, so it returns `nil` by default. The controller then sets `@topic_view = nil` and implicitly renders `best.html.erb`, which calls `@topic_view.posts.present?` — this will raise `NoMethodError` on `nil`, so the subsequent `after` block assertion (`response.should be_success`) can never be reached; the test will error rather than pass/fail meaningfully, meaning the 'creates a topic view when a topic_id is found' path is not actually verified to render correctly.

Unused translation key `embed.permalink`

The new `embed.permalink: "Permalink"` string is added to the locale file but is never referenced by any of the new embed views or controller (`app/views/embed/best.html.erb`, `app/views/embed/loading.html.erb`, `app/controllers/embed_controller.rb`), making it dead i18n content left over from an unfinished feature.

absolutize_urls mangles protocol-relative URLs

`absolutize_urls` treats any `href`/`src` starting with `/` as site-relative and rewrites it by stripping all leading slashes and prepending `prefix + "/"`. Protocol-relative URLs such as `//cdn.example.com/image.png` also start with `/`, so `href.sub(/^\/+/, '')` strips both leading slashes, turning the URL into `cdn.example.com/image.png`, which then becomes `prefix/cdn.example.com/image.png` (e.g. `http://eviltrout.com/cdn.example.com/image.png`) — a broken link to the wrong host instead of the intended absolute external resource. This affects both the `a['href']` and `img['src']` rewriting blocks (lines ~62-73).

feed_key is computed but never used

`feed_key` builds a Redis key intended to track feed modification state (likely for conditional GET / avoiding reprocessing unchanged feeds), but it is never referenced anywhere in `poll_feed` or elsewhere in the job. As written, every hourly poll fully fetches and parses the entire feed and calls `TopicEmbed.import` for every item regardless of whether the feed has changed, which is unnecessary load on the external feed source; the dead `feed_key` method suggests this optimization was intended but not wired up.

raw_html cook method bypasses sanitization for externally-sourced content

`Post#cook` now returns `raw` verbatim (skipping `PrettyText`/`post_analyzer.cook`) when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. This mode is used for all posts created via `TopicEmbed.import` (app/models/topic_embed.rb line 22), including content pulled from `app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb`, which feeds raw RSS/Atom `content` (only `CGI.unescapeHTML`'d, never sanitized) directly into `TopicEmbed.import`. The resulting `cooked` value is later rendered unescaped via `<%= raw post.cooked %>` in app/views/embed/best.html.erb. If the configured feed (or a compromised/hijacked feed source) contains `<script>` or other malicious markup, it will be served verbatim to all visitors of the embed page, bypassing Discourse's normal HTML sanitization pipeline entirely — a stored XSS risk.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is missing the trailing '?' required by the serializer convention

Every other conditional attribute in this file follows the `include_#{attr}?` naming convention (e.g. `include_email?`, `include_card_image_badge_id?`, and the dynamically generated `include_#{attr}?` methods from `staff_attributes`/`private_attributes`/`untrusted_attributes`). The new method is defined as `def include_website_name` (no `?`), so the serializer will never find/call it as the inclusion-guard for the `website_name` attribute. As a result `website_name` is unconditionally included in the serialized output (even as `null` when `website` is blank), ignoring the intended `website.present?` gate. This also means any attempt to hide `website_name` based on trust-level/anonymous rules (see related finding) cannot work even if added, since the guard method itself is never invoked.

false_positives.candidate:
Asymmetric subdomain matching logic in website_name

The matching logic handles the case where the Discourse host has an extra subdomain relative to the website host (e.g. website 'example.com' vs instance 'forums.example.com', tested in spec), via `discourse_host.ends_with?("." << website_host)`. However the reverse case — the website host has an extra subdomain relative to a bare instance domain (e.g. website 'http://forum.example.com' vs instance host 'example.com') — is not handled: the `ends_with?` check is only performed in one direction, so this case falls through without expanding to the full path even though it represents the same underlying domain relationship. This asymmetry is untested and likely not intended given the feature's goal of detecting same-domain websites.

Mutating string literal with << instead of safe concatenation

`discourse_host.ends_with?("." << website_host)` uses the mutating `<<` operator on the string literal `"."` rather than `+` or interpolation. This happens to work today because the file has no `# frozen_string_literal: true` magic comment, but it is fragile: if frozen string literals are enabled for this file in the future (a common Rails convention), this line will raise a `FrozenError` at runtime. It should use `".#{website_host}"` or `"." + website_host` instead.

No test verifying website_name is restricted for TL0/anonymous viewers like website

The 'with a TL0 user seen as anonymous' context (lines 6-16) asserts that `website` and other untrusted attributes are hidden, but does not include `website_name` in `untrusted_attributes` nor set a website on the fabricated user to actually exercise the check. website_name leaks the restricted website attribute to untrusted/anonymous viewers

`website` is listed in `untrusted_attributes` (lines 105-111), which hides it from anonymous viewers when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` is true (e.g. TL0 users). The new derived attribute `website_name` (lines 137-155) is computed directly from `website` via `object.user_profile.website` but is not added to `untrusted_attributes` and has no equivalent restriction check (its `include_website_name` method only checks `website.present?`, not the trust/anonymous restriction). false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.

false_positives.candidate:
Breaking change to /groups/:id/members.json response shape and default page size

The `members` action used to return a plain serialized array for non-automatic groups (unbounded) and only paginated automatic groups at a default limit of 200. It now always returns a hash `{members: [...], meta: {total, limit, offset}}` and defaults to a limit of 50 for every group, automatic or not. Any existing API consumer (mobile apps, external integrations, scripts) that expects the previous array response or expects to receive the full membership list for non-automatic groups will break or silently receive only the first 50 members with no indication that pagination occurred. This is a backward-incompatible API change that is not called out or versioned.

Membership mutation is persisted before the subsequent save-based success/failure check

In `add_members`, `group.add(user)` is called in a loop (which persists the association immediately via the has_many collection), and only afterward is `group.save` checked to decide whether to render success or `render_json_error`. The same pattern exists in `remove_member` with `group.users.delete(user_id)` followed by `group.save`. If `group.save` fails for any unrelated reason (e.g. a validation on the group model), the membership change has already been committed to the database, yet the client is told the operation failed via `render_json_error`, producing an inconsistent/misleading response relative to the actual state of the data.

No spec coverage added for the rewritten /groups/:id/members pagination behavior

The `members` action was substantially rewritten: response shape changed to `{members:, meta:}`, pagination now applies uniformly to automatic and non-automatic groups, and the default limit changed from effectively unlimited (non-automatic) / 200 (automatic) to 50 for all groups. No corresponding spec file (e.g. groups_controller_spec.rb) was added or updated in this PR to verify the new `meta` payload, default/overridden limit and offset behavior, or the total count, leaving this behavior-changing rewrite untested.

No upper bound on client-supplied limit and no validation of offset for /groups/:id/members.json

`limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` and `offset = params[:offset].to_i` are used directly in the query with no maximum cap or minimum validation. A client can request an arbitrarily large `limit` to retrieve an entire (potentially huge, e.g. 'everyone') group's membership in a single request, defeating the purpose of pagination and risking excessive serialization/DB load. A negative `offset` is also not guarded against, which can produce unexpected SQL (Postgres rejects negative OFFSET values), leading to a 500 error for malformed input on this public, non-admin endpoint.

addMembers/removeMember actions silently swallow AJAX failures

Unlike `save` and `destroy`, which attach failure handlers that show a `bootbox.alert` with the server error, the `removeMember` and `addMembers` actions call `this.get('model').removeMember(member)` / `addMembers(usernames)` without attaching any rejection handler. If the request fails (e.g. a 422 for an automatic group, or a network error), the promise rejection is unhandled and the admin receives no feedback that the action did not take effect. Additionally the `addMembers` action leaves a `// TODO: should clear the input` comment, meaning the username input is never cleared after a successful add, which can lead to accidental duplicate submissions.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback chain locales are only pre-loaded in ApplicationController, not everywhere I18n.locale is used

`translate` (and `load_locale`) only loads translation files for `config.locale`, the single currently-active locale. Because `I18n::Backend::Base#load_translations` is patched (line ~25-29 of this file) to be a no-op unless called explicitly, any locale whose files were never explicitly loaded has zero translations in memory, even if the YAML file exists on disk. The new feature relies on `ApplicationController#set_locale` calling `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` to pre-load the whole fallback chain (locale, site default locale, :en) before rendering a web request. But any other code path that sets `I18n.locale` directly – Sidekiq jobs, mailers that iterate per-recipient locales, rake tasks, console sessions – never calls `ensure_loaded!`, so the middle fallback locale (the site default locale) is never loaded there. The fallback module will then raise MissingTranslationData for that un-loaded locale regardless of whether a real translation exists, and silently skip straight to `:en`. This defeats the purpose of the feature for exactly the code paths (background jobs, digest emails) where multi-locale translation matters most.

FallbackLocaleList silently ignores any explicit per-locale fallback configuration

`FallbackLocaleList` subclasses `Hash` but only overrides `#[]`, fully computing `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en]` regardless of hash contents. Standard mutator methods like `[]=`/`store`/`merge!` are still inherited unchanged, so any code (future plugin, console usage, or another part of the app) that tries to customize the fallback chain for a specific locale the normal `I18n.fallbacks` way (e.g. `I18n.fallbacks[:'pt-BR'] = [:pt]`, which works with the standard `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks` Hash-like API) will silently write into the backing Hash but the write is never read back by `[]`. This breaks the expected Hash/fallbacks contract without any error or warning, which can be confusing and hard to debug later.

LRU translation cache can serve stale fallback results after SiteSetting.default_locale changes

The cache key is `"#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}"`, which does not encode which locale a translation was actually resolved through in the fallback chain. With this PR, the fallback chain itself (`FallbackLocaleList#[]` in config/initializers/i18n.rb) depends on the mutable `SiteSetting.default_locale`. If an admin changes the site's default locale at runtime, previously cached entries for keys that were resolved via fallback to the old default locale will continue to be returned from the LRU cache (keyed only by key+locale+backend id) until the backend object changes or the process restarts/`I18n.reload!` is invoked. This produces incorrect, stale fallback translations for an indeterminate period after a site-setting change that used to have no bearing on translation caching before this PR (previously fallback only ever used the fixed `I18n.default_locale` config constant).

New fallback chain drops intermediate language-tag fallback, reducing translation coverage for regional locales

Previously, fallback was enabled via `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` (removed from config/environments/production.rb, profile.rb and the cloud66 config in this PR), which engages Rails/I18n's standard `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks`, computing fallback through locale-tag decomposition (e.g. `:'zh-CN'` -> `:zh` -> default locale). The new `FallbackLocaleList#[]` only returns `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en]`, with no intermediate base-language step. For any regional locale where only the base-language YAML exists (e.g. only `client.zh.yml`, no `client.zh-CN.yml`), lookups that previously fell through to `:zh` will now jump straight from `:'zh-CN'` to the site default locale (often `:en`), losing already-translated strings. The code acknowledges this via a TODO comment but it is still a behavioral regression for users on region-specific locale codes.

No tests added for the new I18n fallback behavior

This PR introduces a new fallback resolution mechanism (`FallbackLocaleList`), a new `I18n.ensure_loaded!`/`I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` loading path, and a behavior change in `ApplicationController#set_locale`, all of which materially change how translations resolve across the whole application. No spec covers that the fallback chain is `[locale, site default, :en]`, that `ensure_loaded!` actually loads the needed locale files, or that translations correctly fall back when a key is missing in the primary locale. Given the wide blast radius of i18n changes, the lack of any automated coverage is a notable gap.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requiring user != null breaks anonymous/discoverable-key passkey login

`isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` returns `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`. This method now gates the calls to `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` in both `authenticate()` (lines 115-117) and `challenge(context, error, field)` (lines 137-140), which are invoked with `context.getUser()` as the argument. Previously, `fillContextForm` was called precisely when `context.getUser() == null` (the normal, anonymous/first-time login case that enables the discoverable-key / conditional UI passkeys flow, e.g. navigator.credentials.get with conditional mediation). With the new `user != null` requirement, `fillContextForm` is now only invoked when a user is already present in the context (the re-authentication case this PR intends to fix), and is skipped entirely for a fresh/anonymous login attempt. This removes the webauthn challenge/rpId/attribute setup needed for the base passkeys login flow, which is exercised by pre-existing tests such as `webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey()` and `passwordLoginWithExternalKey()` in PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest/PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest, that rely on the webauthn form/attributes being present on the very first page load with no pre-selected user. The fix for re-authentication should not have been conditioned on `user != null`; the flag should simply reflect whether passkeys/webauthn is enabled, independent of whether a user has already been resolved.

false_positives.candidate:
Unused import added

The import `org.keycloak.models.credential.PasswordCredentialModel` was added by this PR but is never referenced anywhere in the file's body. This is dead code left over from the change and should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset branch passes a negative start index into Django QuerySet slicing, which Django explicitly rejects

When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with `start_offset = cursor.offset` (negative). Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` for negative slice bounds; it does not 'properly handle negative slicing automatically' as the adjacent comment claims. As a result, the advertised 'negative offset support for efficient reverse pagination' will throw an unhandled exception any time it is exercised (e.g. a client-supplied cursor like `0:-5:0` combined with `optimized_pagination=true`), rather than providing any pagination benefit. The subsequent `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` check also reuses the unclamped, possibly-negative `offset`, compounding the broken logic once/if the slicing issue is fixed.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Possible AttributeError if organization_context.member is None

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` will raise `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'` if `request.user.is_superuser` is False and `organization_context.member` is None (e.g. a non-superuser path that does not guarantee a member record, such as certain token-based or cross-silo access patterns). Other code in the codebase typically guards this with `organization_context.member and organization_context.member.has_global_access`. If this path is reachable, a normal GET request to this endpoint would 500 instead of falling back to standard pagination.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key is incompatible with datetime fields and crashes on any real use

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key() (and value_from_cursor) are copied verbatim from the numeric Paginator implementation: `value = getattr(item, self.key); math.floor(value)`. But the endpoint wires this paginator up with `order_by="-datetime"` (organization_auditlogs.py), so `self.key` is "datetime" and `value` is a `datetime.datetime` instance. `math.floor()`/`math.ceil()` on a `datetime` object raises `TypeError` because datetime defines neither `__floor__` nor `__float__`. `build_cursor()` calls this key function on the first/last result as soon as there is at least one row, so any request to `/organization-audit-logs/?optimized_pagination=true` made by an authorized admin that returns a non-empty result set will raise an unhandled exception (HTTP 500). The entire 'optimized pagination' feature is therefore non-functional for its only real caller.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Importing non-existent OptimizedCursorPaginator

false_positives.candidate:
Comment claims new 'advanced pagination' capability was added here, but no functional change was made

The added comment states 'Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios... This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets', but the line below it (`self.offset = int(offset)`) is unchanged from before the PR — `Cursor` already accepted negative integers via `int()`. The comment implies this file implements/enables a feature, when in fact the (broken) negative-offset handling lives entirely in paginator.py and is unrelated to this cast. This is misleading documentation that doesn't reflect any real change.

Misleading comments overstate Django's slicing capabilities and the safety of the feature

The comments at lines 876 ('The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically') and 879 ('This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level') are factually incorrect/misleading: Django's QuerySet does not support negative slice bounds and will raise ValueError, and the 'safety' claim conflates authorization (who can call this code) with the actual boundary-condition correctness of slicing negative indices, which it is not. These comments will mislead future maintainers trying to understand or debug this code.

New paginator duplicates ~65 lines of BasePaginator.get_result with no actual performance optimization

Despite the PR's title and docstring claiming 'performance optimizations for high-traffic endpoints' and an 'optimized query path for large datasets', `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result()` is a near-verbatim copy-paste of `BasePaginator.get_result()` with one added (and broken, per other findings) branch for negative offsets. It performs the same queries, same hit counting, and same cursor-building as the base class — there is no demonstrated or plausible performance improvement. The duplication also means any future bug fix or improvement made to `BasePaginator.get_result()` will not automatically apply here, creating a maintenance hazard for logic that is already copy-pasted and partially incorrect.

No tests added for the new OptimizedCursorPaginator or the audit log endpoint's new pagination branch

The PR introduces a new paginator class with a non-trivial negative-offset code path, a new `enable_advanced_features` flag, and a new permission-gated branch in `organization_auditlogs.py`, but no tests are included for any of it. Basic tests exercising `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result()` with real `AuditLogEntry` rows (ordered by `-datetime`) or the `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter against the endpoint would have immediately caught the `TypeError` in `get_item_key` and the `ValueError` from negative slicing described in other findings. Given the feature touches shared pagination infrastructure, the lack of coverage is a significant gap before merge.

Unrelated behavioral change to shared BasePaginator.get_result() affects every consumer of Paginator/DateTimePaginator

`BasePaginator.get_result()` is the shared implementation used by `Paginator` and `DateTimePaginator`, which are used by many unrelated list endpoints across the codebase, not just audit logs. This PR changes `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` to clamp the offset via `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, silently changing behavior for any caller that (intentionally or via a malformed cursor) passes a negative offset with `is_prev=False`: previously this would raise (Django disallows negative slice bounds), now it silently starts the page at 0. This is a meaningful behavior change to widely-shared pagination code, introduced only to support a feature that is itself broken (see other findings), with no test coverage and no changelog/documentation of the change. Additionally the accompanying comment says this 'allows negative offsets' when the code actually does the opposite (clamps negative offsets to zero in the non-prev branch), which will mislead future maintainers.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset "advanced pagination" branch is fundamentally broken with Django querysets

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is True and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `start_offset = cursor.offset` and then `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly disallows negative slice indices and raises an exception (`Negative indexing is not supported.`) rather than handling it the way list slicing would. The comment claiming "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is incorrect. As soon as this code path is reached (any authorized user supplies a cursor string with a negative offset while `enable_advanced_features=True`), the request will raise an unhandled exception and return a 500 instead of paginated results, making the entire 'advanced pagination' feature non-functional and a self-inflicted DoS vector for whoever can trigger it.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset clamp only applied for forward pagination, not for prev-cursors

In `BasePaginator.get_result`, the new code clamps `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. This only guards the forward-pagination case; when `cursor.is_prev` is True, the raw (potentially negative, since `Cursor.offset` is parsed directly from user-supplied cursor strings via `int(bits[1])`) offset is passed straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, which will raise an exception on Django querysets. The fix is incomplete/inconsistent: it protects one pagination direction but leaves the other exposed to the same crash.

false_negatives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

false_positives.candidate:
Eviction cap hardcoded to 1000, decoupled from the Python-configurable (and now-unused) max_segment_spans=1001

The eviction threshold `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000) end` is a magic number baked into the Lua script, no longer driven by the `max_segment_spans` setting on `SpansBuffer` (which is unused after this change, see buffer.py finding). The two numbers (1000 here vs. 1001 previously configured in Python) are also off-by-one from each other, making it easy for future maintainers to believe changing `max_segment_spans` has any effect, when it no longer does.

Misleading comment implies a functional change that doesn't exist in this file

The added comment states "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios... This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets," but the code on the next line (`self.offset = int(offset)`) is unchanged from before — `int()` already accepted negative numbers. No validation or enablement logic was added here. The comment is misleading: it suggests this file deliberately sanctions negative offsets as a safe, supported feature, while the actual consumers of `Cursor.offset` (in paginator.py) do not safely support negative values and will raise exceptions when given one. This can mislead future maintainers into believing negative offsets are a vetted, working feature.

New OptimizedCursorPaginator and the audit log endpoint's optimized_pagination flag have no tests

This PR adds a new paginator class (`OptimizedCursorPaginator`) with a security-relevant negative-offset code path, and wires it into `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` behind a new query parameter and an authorization check. No tests were added for either the paginator class or the new endpoint branch (e.g. verifying authorized vs. unauthorized access, or correct/incorrect handling of negative offsets). Given the broken negative-offset handling identified separately, tests would have caught this before merge.

New hard-required field `end_timestamp_precise` with no fallback risks consumer crash on rollout/old messages

`process_batch` now does `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` using direct dict indexing (unlike the optional `val.get("parent_span_id")` pattern used elsewhere). If any in-flight or backlog Kafka message lacks this field (e.g. during a mixed-version rollout where Relay/producers haven't yet guaranteed this field, or on topic replay of older messages), this raises a `KeyError` that is not handled anywhere in this path, which will fail the whole batch and likely crash/stall the consumer. This is a behavior change from the previous code which did not require this key at all.

No test coverage for the new >1000-span eviction behavior added by this PR

The PR's stated purpose is "Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert," implemented via `zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua when a segment's sorted set exceeds 1000 members. None of the changes in this test file add a case that inserts more than 1000 spans into a single segment to verify that the oldest entries are correctly evicted, that the retained spans are the newest ones, or that `flush_segments` behaves correctly afterward. The only changes here are adding the new required `end_timestamp_precise` field to existing unrelated test spans, so the core new behavior of this PR is entirely untested.

Overly broad authorization gate for a pagination path that crashes

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` allows any organization member with "global access" (not just superusers/admins) to opt into `OptimizedCursorPaginator` via the `optimized_pagination=true` query param. The in-code comments describe this as being for "authorized administrators" only, but `has_global_access` is a much weaker bar than superuser. Combined with the broken negative-offset handling in `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (see paginator.py finding), this means a relatively large set of non-admin users can trigger unhandled 500s on this endpoint just by crafting a cursor string, and the intended admin-only restriction is not actually enforced as described.

Redirect-depth safety limit cut 10x without justification or test coverage

The loop bound for resolving the redirect chain was reduced from `0, 10000` to `0, 1000`, and the previous explanatory comment ("theoretically this limit means segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was removed entirely rather than updated. This silently lowers the maximum depth of a redirect/parent chain that can be correctly resolved before the script gives up, risking incorrect segment joining for deeply-nested span trees that previously worked. No test exercises this changed limit, and the change is unrelated to and undocumented in the PR description, which only discusses buffer eviction.

Unrelated, security-sensitive pagination feature bundled into a PR described as a spans-buffer optimization

This PR's title/description describe an optimization to the spans Redis buffer (add-buffer.lua, buffer.py), but it also introduces and wires up an entirely new, broken pagination mechanism (`OptimizedCursorPaginator`, negative-offset cursor handling, and a new `optimized_pagination` endpoint flag in the audit log API) that is unrelated to spans buffering. This combination of an unrelated, under-tested, and crash-prone authorization-adjacent feature with a narrowly-described infra change is the kind of change that should be split into its own PR with explicit review of its authorization model and failure modes; as bundled, it is easy for reviewers focused on the stated spans-buffer change to miss the new attack surface in the pagination code.

max_segment_spans parameter is now dead code, and its prior observability was removed without replacement

`SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans` (default 1001), but after this change nothing in `buffer.py` reads `self.max_segment_spans` anymore. Previously, `_load_segment_data` used this value to detect and skip (with `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded")` and an error log) segments whose span count exceeded the limit. That enforcement and its metric were removed in favor of the Lua script's hard-coded eviction at `span_count > 1000`, but no equivalent metric/log was added for the new eviction path, and the now-unused constructor parameter is misleading to callers/tests who may still pass it expecting enforcement.

zunionstore uses default SUM aggregate, corrupting timestamp scores on overlapping members

After switching the span buffer from Redis sets (`sadd`/`sunionstore`) to sorted sets (`zadd`/`zunionstore`) keyed by `end_timestamp_precise`, the `zunionstore` calls at lines 47 and 53 do not specify `AGGREGATE MIN`, so Redis defaults to `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the same member (identical span payload) exists in both sets being merged — e.g. in the edge case where `parent_span_id == span_id` causes `span_key` to equal `set_key`, or if a span payload is present under more than one bucket due to redirect processing/retries — its score (meant to represent an end timestamp used for both flush-timeout tracking and the new `zpopmin` eviction) gets summed with itself, producing a corrupted, non-timestamp value. This can cause spans to be evicted/retained in the wrong order or to never expire as intended, silently defeating the new eviction logic this PR introduces.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility check uses outer `dataset` instead of the `scoped_dataset` parameter actually being queried

Inside `_get_event_stats(scoped_dataset, query_columns, query, snuba_params, ...)`, the call `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` references the enclosing `dataset` variable computed once in `get()`, not the `scoped_dataset` parameter that is actually used to execute the query (`scoped_dataset.run_top_events_timeseries_query`, `scoped_dataset.top_events_timeseries`, `scoped_dataset.timeseries_query`). In the dashboard-widget discover-split logic (`get_event_stats_factory`), `_get_event_stats` is invoked with varying first arguments (`discover`, `split_dataset`, `scoped_dataset`) that can differ from the outer `dataset`. As a result, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` can make its decision based on the wrong dataset (e.g. outer dataset is `metrics_enhanced_performance` while the actual sub-query runs against `discover` with an error-focused query), causing upsampling to be incorrectly skipped or applied for that sub-query.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

false_positives.candidate:
Broad silent exception swallowing in new test helper

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` wraps both the dict traversal (`normalized_data.get("contexts", {}).get("error_sampling", {}).get("client_sample_rate")`) and the float conversion in bare `except Exception: pass` blocks. Any malformed or unexpected shape of `contexts`/`error_sampling` (e.g. `contexts` explicitly set to `None`) will silently skip setting `sample_rate` with no logging or error surfaced, making it harder to diagnose why upsampling-related fixtures in tests produce unexpected counts if the test data doesn't match the expected shape exactly.

Cache key derived from Python's built-in `hash()` on project id tuples risks collisions across different project sets

`cache_key` is built as `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))}"`. Using the generic `hash()` of a tuple (rather than a stable, collision-free encoding like a joined string of ids) means two different project-id sets within the same organization could theoretically hash-collide, causing the eligibility result computed for one project combination to be served for a different, unrelated combination for up to 60 seconds — i.e. a non-allowlisted project set could incorrectly inherit `True` (or vice versa), producing incorrect (scaled or unscaled) error counts for users.

Docstrings contradict each other regarding cache freshness

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` documents caching the allowlist eligibility result for 60 seconds ("Cache allowlist eligibility for 60 seconds ... eventual consistency is acceptable"), while the helper it calls on a cache miss, `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, states "This function reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time... This is intentional to ensure we always have the latest configuration state." In practice, due to the 60-second cache wrapping it, the configuration is NOT read fresh on every call, contradicting the inner function's documented intent and potentially misleading future maintainers about the actual consistency guarantees.

New `upsampled_count()` aggregate is not marked private, bypassing the allowlist gate

The new SnQLFunction `upsampled_count` (computing `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`) is registered in the public function converter without `private=True`, unlike the function defined immediately above it which does set `private=True`. Because this function is publicly resolvable, any user/org can request it directly (e.g. `yAxis=upsampled_count()` or in `field`), completely bypassing the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` gate implemented in `error_upsampling.py`. For non-allowlisted projects where `sample_weight` is not meaningfully populated, this returns incorrect/misleading aggregate values, and more importantly it exposes an internal column (`sample_weight`) and computation path outside the intended governance of the feature flag/allowlist mechanism.

No fallback/null handling for `sample_weight`, risking silent undercount for pre-upsampling or non-sampled events

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` rewrites `count()` to `upsampled_count() as count` (i.e. `sum(sample_weight)`) for any allowlisted project, with the comment "no additional null checks are needed here" because sample_weight is assumed to exist for all events. If historical events ingested before this feature (or events not going through the client-sampling code path) have `sample_weight` as NULL or unset, `sum()` over those rows effectively treats them as 0 rather than 1, silently undercounting legitimate error events the moment a project is added to the allowlist, with no defensive `coalesce`/default applied in the SnQL (`sum(Column("sample_weight"))` in discover.py).

No tests for the public caching entry point or cache invalidation

The test suite only exercises private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`) but never calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` itself — the function that actually implements the caching behavior described as the PR's core "performance optimization". There is no test validating cache-hit vs cache-miss paths, TTL behavior, or that `invalidate_upsampling_cache` actually clears the correct key. Given the caching logic introduces real correctness risk (stale allowlist decisions, hash-based key collisions), this is the part of the change most in need of direct test coverage, and it currently has none.

Unrelated/accidental file (looks like a git submodule reference) added to the PR

The PR adds a file named `sentry-repo` whose only content is `Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a`, which is characteristic of an accidentally committed git submodule/embedded repository reference rather than an intentional source change. This is unrelated to the stated feature, is not referenced by any other changed file, and risks causing checkout/tooling issues (e.g. "adding embedded git repository" warnings, or broken clones if the referenced commit isn't fetchable as a submodule) for anyone who clones or rebases on top of this commit. It should be removed before merge.

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined but never called anywhere

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is documented as something that "should be called when the allowlist configuration changes to ensure cache consistency", but no code in this PR (or evidently elsewhere) calls it when the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` option changes. This leaves the 60-second TTL as the only consistency mechanism, so removing a project from the allowlist (e.g. to fix an incident or stop a misconfiguration) will continue to serve stale, upsampled/scaled counts for up to 60 seconds with no way to force immediate invalidation, despite the function's docstring implying such a mechanism exists.

TableWidgetVisualization branch renders hard-coded empty data instead of query results

It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
validate_timestamp/validate_age use truthy checks instead of presence checks

BrowserReportSerializer.validate_timestamp checks `self.initial_data.get("age")` and validate_age checks `self.initial_data.get("timestamp")` to enforce that exactly one of the two fields is present. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Analytics event recorded before feature flag and input validation

This means analytics will record an 'assemble' event even for requests that are ultimately rejected with 404 (feature disabled) or 400 (invalid payload), inflating/skewing usage metrics for this event rather than reflecting actual successful or attempted assemble operations.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).

false_positives.candidate:
60s processing deadline may be too tight for a 100-identity chunk doing network calls

check_auth_identities now has `processing_deadline_duration=60` while it is invoked with `chunk_size=100` (the default) and loops over each auth identity calling `check_single_auth_identity`, which in turn calls `provider.refresh_identity(auth_identity)` — a network-bound call to the external SSO/auth provider for each identity. Giving only 60 seconds total to refresh up to 100 identities (effectively ~0.6s per identity including request overhead) risks the task being killed mid-batch under normal network latency, which would abort remaining identity refreshes in that chunk without obvious indication which ones were processed.

Caching/retry safeguards lost when switching from useApiQuery to raw useQuery

The previous implementation called useApiQuery with explicit `staleTime: 0, refetchOnWindowFocus: false, retry: false`. The refactor replaces this with a bare `useQuery({enabled, queryKey, queryFn})` that omits all three options, so the hook now falls back to the QueryClient's global defaults for staleness, window-focus refetching, and retries. This can introduce unwanted retries on failed attribute-key fetches and extra refetches whenever the browser tab regains focus, which the original code explicitly avoided — a behavior regression for a hook used in interactive search/typeahead UI.

Environment filter silently dropped from trace-item attribute key requests

The previous implementation (in useTraceItemAttributeKeys.tsx) explicitly sent `environment: selection.environments` as part of the query to `/organizations/.../trace-items/attributes/`. The new shared `makeTraceItemAttributeKeysQueryOptions` omits the environment parameter entirely, with only a comment stating it's 'left out intentionally as it's not supported'. If the backend endpoint does in fact filter by environment, this is a behavior regression that will cause attribute-key suggestions to no longer respect the user's selected environment(s); this should be confirmed against the backend endpoint's actual support for the parameter.

Migration gutted to a no-op without a corresponding test update

convert_org_saved_searches_to_views in 0920 (like 0917) is reduced to a no-op because "this migration had an error and was never run". For 0917, the matching test file (tests/sentry/migrations/test_0917_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views.py) was removed in this same PR since it asserted the old behavior. No corresponding test file for migration 0920 appears anywhere in this changeset. If such a test exists elsewhere in the repo asserting that running 0920 creates GroupSearchView rows, it will now fail (or pass vacuously) since the migration body no longer performs the transformation — this should be verified/cleaned up the same way 0917's test was.

Overly broad exception handling and non-serializable value in log extra

get_environment_info wraps the whole body in `except Exception as e` and logs at `logger.info` with `extra={"issue_id": issue.id, "error": e}`. Given the security sensitivity (webhook secret, symmetric encryption/decryption) and the data-integrity risk (credential corruption as seen in the bugs above), this is a significant gap that would have caught the shape-mismatch and placeholder-value bugs before merge.
