When calling out to the self-hoster's `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, the request is a plain POST with only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the body — no signature, bearer token, or shared secret (e.g. `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`) is sent. The self-hosted endpoint therefore has no built-in way to verify that the request genuinely originated from this Cal.com instance, unlike the inbound `/api/webhook/app-credential` endpoint, which does require a shared secret. This is a one-sided trust model: any party that can reach the configured endpoint URL can impersonate Cal.com's refresh requests unless the self-hoster independently reinvents authentication, which is not documented anywhere in `.env.example`.

The two files are now inconsistent: if `appConfig.slug` in `config.json` ever changes, the authorize URL and the token-exchange redirect URI would silently diverge, breaking the OAuth flow for this app. This change appears unrelated to the credential-sync feature and looks like an unintended regression introduced by the refactor.

`getClient()` is invoked from the constructor on every `SalesforceCalendarService` instantiation (i.e. on essentially every booking/calendar operation for a Salesforce credential), and it unconditionally POSTs to `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` to refresh the access token — there is no check of token expiry before doing so, unlike every other integration in this codebase (which gate refreshing behind an `isExpired`/`isTokenValid` check). This wastes Salesforce API quota on every call and, since Salesforce issues/may rotate refresh tokens, repeated unnecessary refreshes under concurrent requests can race and invalidate tokens still in use elsewhere. Additionally, unlike all the other apps touched in this PR, this refresh call is not routed through the new `refreshOAuthTokens` helper, so the self-hosted credential-sync feature this PR introduces does not work for Salesforce at all, despite the PR's stated goal of broad app support.

This is vulnerable to timing side-channel attacks that can be used to guess the secret byte-by-byte, especially since the endpoint has no rate limiting. A constant-time comparison (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual`) should be used instead. Additionally, the handler does not check `req.method`, so non-POST requests are processed the same way; a GET/other request without a JSON body will fail the zod `.parse()` with an unhandled exception rather than a clean 405, leaking a generic error instead of a well-defined API contract.

This can make consumer shutdown unexpectedly slow and risks the process being force-killed by orchestration before a graceful stop completes.

close()/terminate() destroy the factory-level shared queue pool, breaking processing after every rebalance

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() and terminate() call self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which shuts down every worker thread and all underlying queues. However, FixedQueuePool is created exactly once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ (result_consumer.py) and is reused unchanged across every subsequent create_with_partitions() call (create_thread_queue_parallel_worker just returns a new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy wrapping the same self.queue_pool). Arroyo's StreamProcessor calls close()/join() on the current strategy on every partition revoke (which happens on every consumer-group rebalance, e.g. deploys/scaling) before calling create_with_partitions() again for the new assignment. Since the pool is never recreated, the new strategy instance submits work into queues that have already been shut down. In FixedQueuePool.submit(), add_offset() runs before work_queue.put(); when put() then fails against the shut-down queue, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()'s except branch calls add_offset()+complete_offset() again, marking the offset as processed even though the message was never handed to a worker. The periodic commit loop then commits these offsets. The net effect is that after the very first rebalance, the consumer silently stops doing any real work while continuing to advance/commit offsets, i.e. permanent, hard-to-notice data loss until logs are inspected.

decode_payload asserts against FilteredPayload, but the queue strategy's decoder contract requires handling it

decode_payload has `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)`. create_thread_queue_parallel_worker passes `partial(self.decode_payload, self.topic_for_codec)` as the `decoder` for SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy, whose declared type is `Callable[[KafkaPayload | FilteredPayload], T | None]` — i.e. it is expected to tolerate FilteredPayload inputs and return None. Instead, any FilteredPayload reaching submit() causes decode_payload to raise AssertionError, which is caught by the generic `except Exception` in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() and logged as 'Error submitting message to queue' even though a filtered payload is an expected, non-error condition. This produces misleading error-level log noise for a normal case and masks real decode errors among the noise.

join(timeout) ignores the supplied timeout and re-runs close() with hard-coded internal timeouts

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(self, timeout=None) simply calls self.close() again, discarding the caller-supplied timeout entirely. close() internally uses fixed 5.0s timeouts for the commit thread join and (via FixedQueuePool.shutdown) for each worker join. This means any operator-configured join timeout (e.g. via the consumer's --join-timeout / join_timeout plumbing in sentry/consumers/__init__.py) has no effect for the thread-queue-parallel mode, and shutdown duration is not actually controlled by the configured value, which can surprise operators expecting a bounded, configurable shutdown.

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts an invariant the implementation does not provide

This test expects that when the first of two same-group messages raises during processing, offsets are not committed (`assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`). However OrderedQueueWorker.run() unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in a `finally` block regardless of whether result_processor raised, so both submitted offsets (100 and 101) become 'complete' and thus committable as soon as the periodic (1s-interval) commit loop runs. Given the test waits up to ~2 seconds for processing/queue-draining before asserting, the commit loop is very likely to have already run and committed by the time the assertion executes, making the assertion either reliably false or flaky depending on timing, rather than verifying a real guarantee.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Check() now performs a full permission re-fetch from DB whenever the cached permission map denies a specific resource

Previously, getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions checked permCache first and returned the cached scope map unconditionally (whether or not it granted the specific requested resource), so a single cached entry served unlimited Check() calls for any resource until TTL expiry. After this change, that internal cache check was removed from getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions; now, whenever getCachedIdentityPermissions finds a cached map but checkPermission against it returns false (resource not found in the cached scope map), Check() falls through and calls getIdentityPermissions again, which unconditionally re-queries permissionStore.GetUserPermissions from the DB. Only the new per-resource permDenialCache prevents repeating this for the exact same resource later. For workflows that call Check() once per resource across many distinct dashboards/folders a user cannot access, each first encounter with a new resource now triggers a full DB permission listing query instead of being resolved for free from the already-valid cached permission map, multiplying DB load compared to before.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key can collide for different (action, name, parent) tuples

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates action, name and parent with a plain '_' delimiter: namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent. Because dashboard/folder UIDs (name, parent) are allowed to contain underscores, two different tuples can produce the exact same string, e.g. (action="dashboards:read", name="a_b", parent="c") and (action="dashboards:read", name="a", parent="b_c") both yield "...perm_<uid>_dashboards:read_a_b_c". Since permDenialCache, permCache, idCache, etc. all share the same underlying cache.Cache instance (only key prefixes differ), this collision causes the cached 'denied' verdict for one resource to be incorrectly applied to a completely different resource/folder combination, producing wrong Check() results for up to the cache TTL.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key uses unresolved subject id, inconsistent with other caches

userPermDenialCacheKey is built from checkReq.UserUID, which is the raw identifier parsed directly from the request subject (could be a numeric legacy ID or a UID depending on caller). All other per-user caches (idCache, permCache, teamCache, basicRoleCache) key on the canonical resolved UID obtained via GetUserIdentifiers. If the same user is referenced by different subject formats across calls (e.g. numeric ID in one call, UID in another), the denial cache entries will not be shared between them, reducing the cache's effectiveness and making its behavior inconsistent with the rest of the caching scheme.

New denial cache can re-introduce the exact bug this PR fixes via a create/permission-grant race

After a real (non-cached) permission check returns not-allowed, Check() unconditionally stores a 'deny' entry (s.permDenialCache.Set) keyed by namespace/user/action/name/parent, and this entry is consulted first on every subsequent Check() for up to shortCacheTTL (30s), short-circuiting before any DB lookup. If a user creates a resource and the authorization check races with the commit of the resource's permission grant (the exact scenario this PR intends to fix), the first Check() can observe no permission yet, be denied, and have that denial cached for 30 seconds — meaning the creator would be locked out of their own newly created dashboard/folder for up to 30 seconds even though permission is already correctly granted moments later. Previously (without this denial cache) each subsequent Check() would simply re-evaluate permissions and succeed as soon as the grant was committed.

No test exercises the write path of the new denial cache

TestService_CacheCheck's "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" test manually seeds s.permDenialCache and verifies that Check() reads it, but no test verifies that Check() actually populates permDenialCache after a genuine denial computed from the store (the new write at service.go's s.permDenialCache.Set call). The existing 'should deny user without permission' test in TestService_Check only checks the response value and never asserts that a subsequent call benefits from (or is affected by) the newly written denial cache entry, leaving this core new behavior without direct coverage.

permissionCacheUsage metric conflates two distinct caches and mislabels cache hits

The permissionCacheUsage metric is incremented with "true" both when the new permDenialCache short-circuits (line ~118) and when the permission cache actually grants access (line ~132), even though these are two separate caches with different semantics. Additionally, when getCachedIdentityPermissions returns a cached map but checkPermission determines the specific resource is not granted, the code unconditionally records permissionCacheUsage "false" (line 137) even though the permission cache was in fact consulted (just insufficient for this resource). This makes the metric unreliable for distinguishing actual cache-miss rates from 'cache hit but resource not covered' cases, undermining monitoring/alerting based on this metric.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing `key` prop for Grafana-origin rule items in FilterView list

In the `rules.map((ruleWithOrigin) => {...})` loop, the 'datasource' and default cases pass `key={key}` to their returned elements, but the 'grafana' case's `<GrafanaRuleListItem .../>` (previously `<GrafanaRuleLoader key={key} .../>`) no longer has a `key` prop set. Since React requires a stable `key` on elements returned directly from a `.map()` callback, this will produce 'Each child in a list should have a unique key prop' warnings and can cause incorrect DOM reuse/reconciliation when the filtered rule list updates (e.g. on refetch or pagination), potentially showing stale rule data for Grafana rules in the filtered/search view.

false_negatives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete menu item is unreachable in the new alert-list flow because it still requires `rulerRule`

`canDelete` is now computed as `(deleteSupported && deleteAllowed) || (grafanaDeleteSupported && grafanaDeleteAllowed)`, so it can become true purely from the new Grafana Prometheus-rule-based ability check (used when only `promRule` is supplied, as is the case for `GrafanaRuleListItem` -> `RuleActionsButtons` in the new alert list view). However the actual render condition is `{canDelete && rulerRule && (...)}`, and `rulerRule` is never passed in that new flow (GrafanaRuleListItem only passes `promRule`). As a result, even users with Delete permission will never see the Delete menu item for Grafana rules rendered via the new list view, even though the ability computation says they should be able to delete. This is confirmed by the new test in GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx ('should render correct menu actions when More button is clicked'), which grants `AlertingRuleDelete` but asserts exactly 4 menu items (no Delete).

`provenance?: string` was added to `GrafanaPromRuleDTOBase` and is now the sole mechanism used by `isProvisionedPromRule()` (utils/rules.ts) to flag a rule as provisioned/immutable in the new alert-list flow, replacing the previous Ruler-based provenance check (`rulerRule.grafana_alert.provenance`). This PR contains no backend changes to the Grafana Prometheus rules endpoint that would populate this field. If the backend does not actually return `provenance` in that API response, `isProvisionedPromRule` will always evaluate to false, causing provisioned (e.g. Terraform/API-managed) alert rules to be incorrectly treated as editable/deletable/duplicable from the UI, which is a data-integrity and governance risk.

Pause ability computed via promRule is dead code; can cause a stray empty divider

`canPause` can now become true solely via the new `grafanaPauseAbility` (promRule-based) check, but the Pause menu item is still gated by `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`, which is always false in the new alert-list flow because `rulerRule` is never supplied there. This means the Pause option can never actually render in that flow despite `canPause` being true, making the promRule-based pause computation effectively dead code. Worse, `canPause` still feeds into `showDivider` (`[canPause, canSilence, ..., canDuplicate].some(Boolean) && [canExport].some(Boolean)`), so when `canPause` is true but nothing else above it renders, an extra/empty `<Menu.Divider />` can appear with nothing above it in the dropdown.

Rule view link no longer carries the `returnTo` parameter, breaking back-navigation

The removed `GrafanaRuleLoader.tsx` built the rule-detail link with `createRelativeUrl('/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view', { returnTo })`, where `returnTo` came from `createReturnTo()` so the detail page could navigate back to the originating list/filter view. The new `GrafanaRuleListItem.tsx` builds the href as `createRelativeUrl('/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view')` with no `returnTo` and no import of `useReturnTo`/`createReturnTo` at all. Users navigating from the alert list to a rule's detail page will lose the ability to return to their previous filtered/list view context.

Transient 'Creating'/'Deleting' states for Grafana rules are removed without replacement

The previous implementation fetched both the Ruler group and the Prometheus group and used `matchRules()` to show a 'Creating' indicator for rules present in the Ruler but not yet reflected by Prometheus, and a 'Deleting' indicator (via `RuleOperationListItem`) for rules still present in Prometheus after being removed from the Ruler. This PR removes the Ruler fetch and the matching logic entirely (and the corresponding `matchRules` unit tests), so during the eventual-consistency window after creating or deleting a Grafana rule, the list will simply omit or show stale rules with no visual indication of the pending state, which is a UX regression compared to the previous behavior and is not covered by any new test.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Interpolating queries before the $__range exclusion check breaks splitting-safety for $__range queries

In runSplitQuery(), queries are now interpolated via datasource.applyTemplateVariables() (line 299) before being passed to querySupportsSplitting()/isQueryWithRangeVariable() (lines 282-289, used at line 300). isQueryWithRangeVariable() is a textual check for the literal `$__range` placeholder in query.expr. Because interpolation now runs first, any `$__range` usage is already replaced with a concrete value (computed for the original, un-split overall range) before this check executes, so the literal text is gone and isQueryWithRangeVariable() will always return false post-interpolation. As a result, queries that use `$__range` - which the code comment explicitly says must be excluded from time splitting because the backend would otherwise interpolate the range variable using each split sub-range - are no longer routed into `nonSplittingQueries`. Instead they are split normally, and every sub-request ends up reusing the single baked-in value computed for the full original range (e.g. a 3-day range baked into `[3d]`) even though each sub-request only covers a fraction of that range (e.g. 1 day). This silently produces incorrect query results (wrong window/rate calculations) for any metric/log query relying on `$__range`, and effectively makes the exclusion logic in querySupportsSplitting() dead code.

No regression test for $__range queries after moving interpolation earlier

The new 'Interpolates queries before execution' test only exercises variable interpolation for `$__auto` and `$step`, which are unrelated to time-range splitting decisions. There is no test verifying that queries containing `$__range` are still excluded from time splitting (routed to nonSplittingQueries) after interpolation now runs before the querySupportsSplitting/isQueryWithRangeVariable check. Given that this reordering can break that exclusion (see related finding), a regression test asserting that `$__range` queries are not split, and that the correct non-split range interpolation is preserved, is missing and would have caught this issue.

applyTemplateVariables is now invoked redundantly multiple times for the same query in the shard-splitting path

runShardSplitQuery() interpolates all targets via datasource.applyTemplateVariables() (line 52) before delegating to splitQueriesByStreamShard(), which for every shard group/cycle calls runSplitQuery() (querySplitting.ts line 163-166) - and runSplitQuery() itself now also calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables() on its targets (querySplitting.ts line 299). The already-interpolated query is therefore re-interpolated once more for every sub-request that the sharding loop produces. This is confirmed by the updated test in shardQuerySplitting.test.ts (line 112), which now expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times for a single input query (1 initial call + 4 sub-request calls) instead of once as before. Besides the unnecessary repeated work, this is risky if applyTemplateVariables is not fully idempotent (e.g. if it injects ad-hoc filters into the expr string), since re-running it on an already-processed query could duplicate ad-hoc filter matchers or otherwise produce different results depending on context (scopedVars/time range) available at each call site.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
traceID no longer included in 'Plugin Request Completed' log line

The previous implementation of logRequest explicitly extracted the trace ID via `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` and appended it as a `traceID` log field. This PR removes that logic entirely (the `tracing` import was dropped from this file) and the new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware.instrumentContext` that replaces the removed context-enrichment code only adds `endpoint`, `pluginId`, `dsName`, `dsUID` and `uname` - it does not add `traceID`. Unless the underlying infra logger automatically injects trace IDs from the context (not evidenced anywhere in this diff), this change silently drops trace correlation information from the 'Plugin Request Completed' log entries, which is a regression for anyone correlating logs with traces.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext discards state, making contextual logging unverifiable in tests

`TestLogger.FromContext` always returns a brand-new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()`, rather than returning the receiver `f` (or otherwise preserving the recorded `InfoLogs`/`WarnLogs`/etc. fields). Since `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` now calls `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)` instead of logging directly on `m.logger`, any test that uses `TestLogger` to assert on the 'Plugin Request Completed' log output (e.g. checking `InfoLogs.Calls`/`Message`) will observe no change on the original logger instance, because the actual `Info` call lands on a disposable, unreferenced `TestLogger` returned by `FromContext`. This effectively makes `TestLogger` unusable for verifying any code path that logs via `FromContext`, which is now the primary logging path for plugin client middlewares.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
Missing documentation of required middleware ordering

The previous `InstrumentationMiddleware` had an explicit comment stating it must be placed at the top of the middleware stack because it both records metrics and enriches the context with a contextual logger. After this refactor, `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` must still be placed before `LoggerMiddleware` (and any other middleware that wants the enriched contextual logger) in the stack for the logging to pick up the attributes via `FromContext`. This ordering constraint is no longer documented anywhere (neither on `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` nor on `LoggerMiddleware`), making it easy for a future change to reorder middlewares (e.g. in pluginsintegration.go) and silently lose the contextual log attributes without any test or compiler error to catch the regression.

New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no unit tests

This PR introduces a brand-new middleware, `ContextualLoggerMiddleware`, which is responsible for enriching the context with plugin/request attributes used by downstream logging (notably `LoggerMiddleware`, which now relies on `FromContext(ctx)` to pick up these attributes). No test file (e.g. contextual_logger_middleware_test.go) was added to verify that QueryData/CallResource/CheckHealth/CollectMetrics correctly attach the expected contextual attributes, or that SubscribeStream/PublishStream/RunStream intentionally do not. Given that this logic was previously covered indirectly inside the (deleted) instrumentation middleware tests, extracting it into its own middleware without dedicated tests leaves this behavior unverified.

Test function name not updated after Instrumentation→Metrics rename

The file was renamed from instrumentation_middleware_test.go to metrics_middleware_test.go and the helper `newInstrumentationMiddleware` call site was updated to `newMetricsMiddleware`, but the test function itself is still named `TestInstrumentationMiddleware`. This is inconsistent with the stated goal of the PR ('Renamed instrumentation middleware to metrics middleware') and leaves stale naming that should have been updated to `TestMetricsMiddleware` for consistency with the rest of the rename.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TOCTOU race allows exceeding the configured device limit

In CreateOrUpdateDevice, the device count is read via CountDevices and then, based on that snapshot, the code decides whether to insert a new device or fall back to update-only. These two steps (count check and insert) are not executed in a single transaction/lock. Under concurrent anonymous requests from different new devices arriving close together, multiple goroutines/requests can all observe count < deviceLimit and all proceed to insert, allowing the actual number of devices to exceed the configured limit. Since the feature's entire purpose is to cap the number of anonymous devices, this race undermines the guarantee the limit is supposed to provide.

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Anonymous device tagging changed from fire-and-forget to synchronous, blocking authentication on a DB round-trip

Previously TagDevice was invoked in a background goroutine with its own timeout, so a failure or latency in anon_device writes never affected the anonymous request itself (errors were only logged). Now TagDevice is awaited synchronously inside Authenticate, so every first-seen device for every anonymous request blocks on a DB count+insert/update before the request can proceed, and any DB error/latency now directly affects anonymous authentication latency and availability (not just the tagging feature). This is a meaningful behavior/availability change for the anonymous auth path that should be called out and load-tested, since anonymous access is often used for public/embedded dashboards with high request volume.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Local cache is set before the DB write succeeds, letting a device bypass the device limit on retry

tagDeviceUI calls a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) immediately, before calling anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. If CreateOrUpdateDevice returns anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached (new behavior added by this PR), tagDeviceUI still leaves the cache entry set. On the next request from the same device (within the ~29 minute cache TTL), the early 'if _, ok := a.localCache.Get(key); ok { return nil }' check short-circuits and returns nil without ever calling CreateOrUpdateDevice again. As a result TagDevice returns nil, client.Anonymous.Authenticate() sees no error, and the device is authenticated successfully even though it was never persisted to anon_device and the device limit was exceeded on its first attempt. This defeats the device limit: a rejected device only needs to retry once to be let in, and will never actually be counted/limited again until the cache entry expires.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

New auth.anonymous device_limit setting is not documented

A new configuration key `device_limit` under `[auth.anonymous]` is introduced (parsed via anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)) and exposed through Cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit, but no corresponding entries were added to conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini, or the configuration reference docs in this PR. No test coverage for Authenticate() rejecting anonymous auth when the device limit is reached

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Routine, successful batch cleanup progress logged at Error level with full ID list dumps

In `CleanAnnotations` (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` (lines 576, 579), every successful batch iteration logs via `r.log.Error(...)` even though no error occurred (the `err` field logged is always nil at that point, since the function already returned early on error). true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.

Cleanup loop ticker interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute without justification

The ticker driving `CleanUpService.Run` was changed from `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` to `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)`. Quadratic string concatenation when building SQLite literal ID list

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Wrong label value (object name instead of resource kind) passed to storage duration metric

In DualWriterMode3.Delete, the successful-path metric call is `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` (line 106), passing the individual object's `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind` (the resource kind, e.g. "playlists"). Since `name` varies per deleted object, this will create a distinct Prometheus label value per object name, causing unbounded metric cardinality and breaking any dashboards that group by resource kind for delete operations. The failure path on line 103 correctly uses `options.Kind`, confirming this is an inconsistency/bug rather than intentional.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive their timeout context from the request context, which is canceled once the handler returns

Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection (lines 51, 110, 135, 163) each spawn a goroutine that does `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, ...)` using the inbound request `ctx` as the parent. For an HTTP server, the request context is canceled once the handler (ServeHTTP) returns; since these methods return the Storage result to the caller immediately after launching the goroutine (without waiting), the apiserver handler will typically finish and the request context will be canceled shortly afterward — well before the 10 second timeout and often before the legacy write even completes. Because cancellation propagates to the derived timeout context, the "safety measure" asynchronous write to legacy storage can be silently aborted on effectively every request, defeating the purpose of mode 3's async legacy write. The goroutine should detach from request cancellation (e.g. use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` or a fresh context carrying only the needed values) before applying its own timeout.

Duplicate entry added to go.work.sum

The diff adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod h1:DkxMin+qOh1Fgkxfbt+CUfBqqsCQJMG9op8Os/irBPA=` as a new line even though an identical entry already exists a few lines above (unchanged). Having a duplicate checksum line suggests the file was not cleanly regenerated via `go work sync`/tooling, which can mask inconsistencies in a manually-edited lock file.

Legacy write errors are silently swallowed (no logging) in async goroutines

In the async legacy-write goroutines for Create (line 56), Delete (line 113), Update (line 140), and DeleteCollection (line 166), the only outcome recorded on failure is a boolean passed into the duration metric (`d.recordLegacyDuration(errObjectSt != nil, ...)`); none of them call `log.Error(...)` the way the previous Mode3 implementation did (e.g. "could not update object in legacy store"). Operators now have no way to see which object/resource failed to replicate to legacy storage except by correlating metrics, substantially reducing observability for a feature explicitly intended as a safety net against unified-storage/legacy divergence.

No test waits for or verifies the asynchronous legacy write actually occurs

None of the Mode3 tests (Create, Delete, Update, DeleteCollection) synchronize with the goroutine that performs the async legacy write, nor do they call `m.AssertExpectations`/`AssertCalled` to confirm `Legacy.*` was actually invoked. Since the goroutine may run after the subtest has already returned, the tests effectively never verify the core new behavior this PR introduces (asynchronous write-through to legacy storage as a safety measure); a regression that removed the legacy write entirely would not be caught by this test suite.

Storage.Create failure recorded under legacy metrics instead of storage metrics

In DualWriterMode3.Create, when d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` (line 45) instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. This mislabels a Storage (unified store) failure as a Legacy failure in the dual-writer metrics, corrupting the error-rate dashboards/alerts that distinguish unified-storage health from legacy-storage health. The same mistake is repeated in Update (line 129).

Storage.Update failure recorded under legacy metrics instead of storage metrics

In DualWriterMode3.Update, when d.Storage.Update fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. This duplicates the same mislabeling bug found in Create (line 45): a Storage failure is reported as a Legacy failure, which will skew metrics used to monitor the health of each backend independently.

TestMode3_Delete never mocks Legacy.Delete even though it is always invoked

DualWriterMode3.Delete unconditionally spawns a goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.Delete(...)` after a successful Storage.Delete. The `testCase` struct in TestMode3_Delete only has a `setupStorageFn` field (no `setupLegacyFn`), so for the "deleting an object in the unified store" success case the legacy mock (`m := &mock.Mock{}`, never associated with `t` via `.Test(t)`) has no registered expectation for `Delete`. Calling an unmocked method on a `testify` mock without `.Test(t)` set panics; since this call happens in a background goroutine, an unrecovered panic there crashes the entire test binary non-deterministically, rather than failing just this test. The test needs to register a Legacy.Delete expectation (and ideally await/verify the call) for success cases.

TestMode3_DeleteCollection never mocks Legacy.DeleteCollection even though it is always invoked

Same issue as in TestMode3_Delete: DualWriterMode3.DeleteCollection always spawns a goroutine calling `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection(...)` after a successful Storage.DeleteCollection, but the `testCase` struct here only defines `setupStorageFn`; there is no `setupLegacyFn` and no `m.On("DeleteCollection", ...)` registered on the legacy mock for the success case. The unmocked call made from the background goroutine will panic in testify's mock (since the mock is not bound to `t`), risking an unrecovered panic that crashes the test process.

Update no longer guarantees the same resolved object is written to both stores

The previous Mode3.Update implementation fetched the current object from Storage, resolved `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)` once, and wrapped the already-resolved object so that both Storage.Update and Legacy.Update applied the exact same final object. The new implementation instead calls `d.Storage.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` and then, in the async goroutine, calls `d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` with the same unresolved `objInfo` (line 139). Each backend will internally invoke `objInfo.UpdatedObject` against its own "old" object; for patch-style updates (merge patch, strategic merge patch, JSON patch) this can produce two different resulting objects if the legacy store's and unified store's current state differ even slightly, causing silent divergence between the two stores — the exact problem dual-writing is meant to prevent. Additionally, invoking `UpdatedObject` a second time may not be safe/idempotent for all `rest.UpdatedObjectInfo` implementations.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing double-check of cache after acquiring write lock

After the first (read-locked) check of entryPointAssetsCache fails (e.g., cache not yet populated or cfg.Env == Dev), the code acquires the write lock at line 48 but never re-checks whether another goroutine already populated the cache while waiting for the lock. As a result, under concurrent initial requests (common right after startup), multiple goroutines can all proceed past the first check, serialize on the write lock, and each redundantly re-read and re-parse assets-manifest.json (or hit the CDN) even though the first goroutine already finished and stored a valid result. This doesn't reintroduce the data race, but it defeats part of the purpose of caching and wastes I/O/CPU under load. A standard fix is to re-check `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` immediately after acquiring the write lock and return early if so.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
No regression test added for the data race fix

The PR fixes a data race on the global entryPointAssetsCache variable in GetWebAssets, but no test was added (e.g., a test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently from multiple goroutines, intended to be run with `go test -race`) to guard against regressions. Without such a test, a future refactor could silently reintroduce the race with no automated signal.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions() contains dead, misleading logic that always returns false

The new helper `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then both the `if enabled` branch and the fallthrough path return `false`. The computed `enabled` value is never actually used to decide the return value — the function unconditionally returns `false` no matter what the feature toggle is set to. While the net effect (always disabling SQL expressions) matches the PR's stated goal, the code reads as if it is checking the feature flag when it is not, and there is no comment explaining that this is an intentional, permanent kill-switch. A future contributor who 'simplifies' this apparent dead code (e.g. by returning `enabled` directly) could unknowingly re-enable the vulnerable code path review intended to permanently disable. This should either be a plain `return false` with an explanatory comment referencing the CVE, or the SQL query type should be removed from the switch entirely.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No tests added for the new SQL-expressions kill switch, and existing tests likely broken

This PR fundamentally changes SQL expression behavior (TablesList/RunCommands/QueryFramesInto now always return "not implemented", and ReadQuery now always errors for QueryTypeSQL), but none of the changed files are tests. Given there must be pre-existing tests exercising pkg/expr/sql/parser.go (TablesList) and pkg/expr/sql_command.go (NewSQLCommand/Execute) that previously asserted correct DuckDB-based behavior (e.g. extracting table names, running real queries), those tests would now fail against the stubbed-out DB that always returns errors, since they are not included/updated in this diff. Conversely, no new test verifies that SQL expressions are now reliably blocked regardless of the FlagSqlExpressions toggle value (i.e., a regression test for the security fix itself is missing). For a PR whose entire purpose is to close an RCE/LFI vulnerability, lacking a test asserting the vulnerable path is unreachable is a significant gap that risks silent regression in future refactors.

false_positives.candidate:
Error message "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is misleading

When QueryTypeSQL is requested, ReadQuery now returns the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented". This is factually incorrect — SQL Expressions were implemented and are being deliberately disabled for security reasons (RCE/LFI, per CVE-2024-9264), not because the feature was never built. Users/administrators who previously had FlagSqlExpressions enabled and relied on it will see a confusing message implying the feature never existed, rather than a clear message indicating it has been disabled. This can misdirect support/debugging efforts and should be reworded (and ideally referenced in release notes/changelog, since this is a breaking change for anyone who had the toggle on).

Leftover "duckDB" variable name contradicts stated PR goal of removing DuckDB references

The PR description states the goal is to "Remove reference to DuckDB", yet the local variable in TablesList is still named `duckDB` (`duckDB := NewInMemoryDB()`) even though it now constructs the stub `sql.DB`, not a DuckDB instance. This is purely cosmetic but is inconsistent with the PR's own stated intent and could confuse future readers into thinking real DuckDB code still exists here.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BuildIndex no longer serializes concurrent builds for the same key

The previous implementation locked cacheMu for the entire BuildIndex call, which (while slow) also serialized concurrent build attempts for the same NamespacedResource key. Now the lock only protects the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write. getOrCreateIndex() in search.go has no locking either (it just checks GetIndex() for nil and calls build() if so), so two concurrent calls for the same cold key (e.g. two simultaneous Search requests, or a Search racing with a watch event) can both perform a full BuildIndex, each creating its own bleve.Index (including on-disk files for file-backed indexes), and whichever finishes last silently overwrites b.cache[key]; the loser's index/resources are never closed or cleaned up, leaking file handles/disk usage and duplicating work.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs() reads cache map without holding cacheMu, racing with BuildIndex writes

TotalDocs() iterates over b.cache with `for _, v := range b.cache` without acquiring cacheMu (neither RLock nor Lock), while BuildIndex now writes to the same map under cacheMu.Lock() after doing the (now unlocked) expensive build work concurrently. Since BuildIndex calls can run concurrently for different keys (that is the whole point of this PR's locking change) and TotalDocs can be invoked at the same time (e.g. the search.go init() logging call right after group.Wait(), or any external caller/metrics path), this is an unsynchronized concurrent map read/write. Go maps are not safe for concurrent read/write; this can produce a 'fatal error: concurrent map read and map write' crash, not just a benign race. GetIndex already correctly uses RLock for cache reads; TotalDocs should do the same.

false_positives.candidate:
NewResourceServer now blocks synchronously on full index build

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) before returning, and Init() runs the full search index build for every namespace (searchSupport.init). Previously NewResourceServer returned immediately and Init() was deferred to the first gRPC call. Index building can take a long time (this is exactly the problem the PR is trying to avoid inside gRPC request contexts), so now the constructor itself can block for an arbitrarily long time, and will fail outright (returning nil, err) if anything in Init fails. Any caller of NewResourceServer that expects a cheap/fast constructor (process startup with readiness/liveness timeouts, module startup sequencing, tests) can now time out or fail to start. The PR description itself asks 'what could this break?' which indicates this tradeoff was not fully evaluated; no caller-side timeout/async handling was added to accommodate the new blocking behavior.

Parallel index build goroutines race on shared err and counter variables

In searchSupport.init(), the errgroup loop spawns one goroutine per namespace (group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers) allows real concurrency) and each goroutine does `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...); return err`, where both `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` are variables captured from the enclosing scope and written concurrently by multiple goroutines without any mutex/atomic. This is a data race: concurrent non-atomic increments of totalBatchesIndexed can lose updates, and concurrent writes to the shared `err` mean a goroutine's `return err` can read a value written by a different goroutine between assignment and return, causing errgroup to receive an incorrect per-goroutine result (e.g. returning another goroutine's error for a successful build, or masking a real failure with nil from a later successful goroutine). This can cause init() to incorrectly fail startup, or silently swallow a failed index build. Each goroutine should use its own local err variable and totalBatchesIndexed should be an atomic counter or protected by a mutex.

Postgres integration test skipped instead of fixed, masking potential regression

The test now unconditionally skips when dbType == 'postgres' with the comment 'test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.' This removes CI coverage of the storage-server module startup path for Postgres, one of the supported production databases, right in the same PR that changes resource-server initialization to run synchronously and eagerly at construction time. Skipping rather than diagnosing/fixing risks hiding a real regression introduced by the eager-Init change (e.g., startup taking too long or behaving differently under Postgres in CI) and leaves no coverage to catch future regressions on that backend until the TODO is addressed.

Trace-context propagation fix applied inconsistently within the same file

The PR fixes span propagation in GetResourceStats by reassigning `ctx, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` so the span is attached to the context used by the subsequent DB call. However, sibling methods in the same file with the identical bug were left unfixed, e.g. ReadResource (line 353: `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, tracePrefix+".Read")`, followed by `b.db.WithTx(ctx, ...)` using the original, span-less ctx), WriteEvent (line ~158), and ListIterator (line ~388). Since the PR's stated goal is 'fixes trace propagation by passing span contexts down', leaving these other call sites with the same discarded-context pattern means their DB operations still won't appear nested under their respective spans in traces, contradicting the PR's intent and leaving inconsistent tracing behavior in the same backend file.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.
Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.

false_positives.candidate:
Inconsistent wrapped vs raw model comparison in login-cache invalidation on update

In update(), `idpById = getById(model.getInternalId())` returns an organization-aware wrapped IdentityProviderModel whose isEnabled() also factors in the linked organization's enabled state (see createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel), while `model` (the second argument passed straight through to registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate) is the raw, unwrapped model from the caller whose isEnabled() reflects only the stored 'enabled' attribute. Because getLoginPredicate() tests ENABLED via isEnabled(), comparing the wrapped 'original' against the raw 'updated' is inconsistent: when the organization is disabled, idpById.isEnabled() can be false even though the stored attribute is true, causing registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate to conclude 'no login-eligibility change' and skip cache invalidation even though the raw 'enabled' attribute genuinely changed. Since the underlying idpDelegate.getForLogin() query filters by the raw stored attribute (not the wrapped value), the cached ID list for getForLogin can become stale and keep referencing an IDP whose real enabled flag changed, violating the documented getForLogin() contract that only enabled/eligible IDPs are returned for callers that don't re-check isEnabled() themselves.

Login-eligibility logic duplicated between getForLogin() search options and getLoginPredicate()

The default getForLogin() method (lines 165-184) determines login eligibility by building search-option maps (LoginFilter.getLoginSearchOptions() plus explicit ORGANIZATION_ID/BROKER_PUBLIC handling), while the new getLoginPredicate() (lines 252-256) re-implements the same eligibility rules as a Predicate for use purely in cache-invalidation decisions in InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider. These two independent representations of the same business rule must be kept manually in sync; if either is changed in the future without updating the other, the Infinispan cache invalidation logic will silently diverge from the actual query semantics, resulting in stale or incorrect getForLogin() cache results.

No test covers organization enable/disable or removal affecting the new getForLogin cache

testCacheIDPForLogin only exercises create/update/remove on the IdentityProvider itself to verify cache invalidation of the new getForLogin caches. It never tests disabling/enabling the linked Organization or removing the Organization entirely. This matters because OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean.java was specifically changed in this PR to re-check idp.isEnabled() at render time precisely because toggling an organization's enabled flag does not invalidate the getForLogin ID-list cache. There is no test verifying that disabling an organization correctly excludes its IDPs from login, nor that removing an organization properly invalidates/cleans up the new login caches for its linked IDPs, leaving this behavior unverified.

Unconditional extra backing-store lookup added to remove()

In remove(), `IdentityProviderModel storedIdp = idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias);` is now called unconditionally before the isInvalid(cacheKey) check. Previously, when the cache entry was valid (`isInvalid(cacheKey)==false`), the method only consulted the local cache (`realmCache.getCache().get(cacheKey, ...)`) and never hit the delegate/JPA store in that branch. Now every remove() call performs an extra delegate lookup even when the cached CachedIdentityProvider already holds the needed model (available via `cached.getIdentityProvider()` in the else branch), adding an avoidable database round-trip to every IDP removal.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() does not return a BouncyCastle provider, violating the interface contract

CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() is documented as returning "BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider". This implementation instead returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is simply whatever JCA provider backs the JVM's default keystore type (e.g. SUN/SunJSSE for 'pkcs12' or 'jks'), unrelated to BouncyCastle. Any shared keycloak-core code path that calls this method expecting an actual BC(-FIPS) provider (e.g. to perform signature/key operations that require BC-specific algorithm support) will silently get the wrong provider instead of a clear failure, which can cause subtle incorrect behavior rather than an explicit error.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code in concatenatedRSToASN1DER

In concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the lines `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` create two throwaway ASN1Encoder instances, write to them, and discard the result without ever using it. This is leftover/dead code that serves no purpose and should be removed before merge; it suggests the implementation was not fully cleaned up.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Indefinite-length ASN.1 encoding not rejected, silently mis-parses malformed sequences

readLength() returns -1 for the BER indefinite-length form (0x80) without raising an error, but DER (which is what ECDSA signatures must use) never permits indefinite length. In readSequence(), the loop condition `while (length > 0)` treats a -1 length as "already done", silently producing an empty element list instead of rejecting the malformed/non-DER input outright. The subsequent `seq.size() != 2` check in AuthzClientCryptoProvider happens to catch this particular case, but the decoder itself does not validate or reject indefinite-length encodings, which is a correctness gap for an ASN.1 DER parser handling externally-supplied signature bytes.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract method order() breaks binary/source compatibility for existing implementers

CryptoProvider is a public SPI interface loaded via ServiceLoader; adding a new abstract method order() (without a default implementation) means any existing third-party or external implementation of CryptoProvider will fail to compile/implement the interface until updated. All in-repo implementers were updated in this PR, but any external module implementing this interface (which is exactly the scenario this PR is designed to support, e.g. authz-client) will break unless it also adds order(). A default method (e.g. returning a baseline value) would preserve compatibility while still allowing providers to opt into custom ordering.

false_positives.candidate:
Inconsistent use of KeystoreFormat.name() instead of toString()

getKeyStore() here calls `KeyStore.getInstance(format.name())`, whereas DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all use `format.toString()`. If KeystoreUtil.KeystoreFormat ever overrides toString() to map enum constants to different keystore type strings, this implementation would silently diverge from the other providers and could request the wrong keystore type. Even if currently harmless, it is an inconsistency that should match the pattern used elsewhere in the codebase.

No test coverage for the new order()-based provider selection logic

This PR's core mechanism change (allowing multiple CryptoProvider instances on the classpath and resolving via order(), replacing the previous exception-on-conflict behavior) has no accompanying unit test. There is no test verifying that the highest-order provider is chosen when multiple providers are present, nor one covering the tie-breaking behavior when providers share the same order value. Given this is a behavior-changing core feature (and a security-relevant one, since it silently resolves what used to be a hard error), it should be covered by dedicated tests in common's test sources.

Silent resolution of multiple CryptoProviders removes a fail-fast safety check

Previously, detectProvider() threw an IllegalStateException if more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classloader, forcing operators to fix a misconfigured classpath (e.g. accidentally shipping both DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider together). The new code silently keeps only the highest-order provider and logs the ignored ones at debug level only (logger.debugf), which is typically disabled in production. All three built-in providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) use the same order()=200, so if two of them end up on the same classpath by mistake, selection among ties depends on ServiceLoader iteration order (jar/classpath ordering), which is not guaranteed to be deterministic across environments. For FIPS-sensitive deployments this can silently select a non-FIPS-compliant provider instead of failing loudly as before, which is a meaningful regression in safety/compliance guarantees without any visible warning.

Unconditional CryptoIntegration.init() now exposes a crypto provider with mostly unimplemented operations

AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now always calls CryptoIntegration.init(), which, for real consumers of the published org.keycloak:keycloak-authz-client artifact, will typically resolve to AuthzClientCryptoProvider as the only CryptoProvider on the classpath (since it has the lowest order=100 and is meant to be overridden when a full provider like DefaultCryptoProvider is also present, which downstream consumers are unlikely to bundle). That provider throws UnsupportedOperationException for the majority of CryptoProvider methods (getAlgorithmProvider, getCertificateUtils, getPemUtils, getOCSPProver, getIdentityExtractorProvider, createECParams, getKeyPairGen, getKeyFactory, getAesCbcCipher/getAesGcmCipher, getSecretKeyFact, getX509CertFactory, getCertStore, getCertPathBuilder, getSignature, wrapFactoryForTruststore). Any current or future authz-client code path (or shared keycloak-core code invoked by it) that relies on these operations will now fail at runtime with UnsupportedOperationException instead of either working (if it didn't previously touch CryptoIntegration) or failing clearly at startup.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Provider event listener now gated by ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1), silently skipping cleanup when only V2 is enabled

The whole body of registerListener's onEvent was wrapped with `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))`. However, `management()`/`evaluator()` elsewhere in this same file only check `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2`, and `AdminPermissionsSchema.isAdminPermissionsEnabled()` also only checks the V2 feature — V2 can be enabled independently of V1. With this guard, realms that only enable ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 (not the legacy V1 feature) will no longer process RoleRemovedEvent, ClientRemovedEvent, or GroupRemovedEvent at all, whereas before this change they always were. This appears to have been added only to avoid calling the new ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled(), which throws UnsupportedOperationException, but the chosen fix disables event handling for roles and groups too (whose management() implementations are not overridden in V2 and would not have thrown). The consequence is that removing a role or group under a V2-only configuration no longer disables the associated permission state, leaving stale permission data behind.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission() relies on resource type tagging that individually-created client resources never receive

getClientsWithPermission() calls `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)` to enumerate resources of type "Clients" and check granted scopes on each. However, AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource() (lines 101-111) creates per-object resources via `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId())` without ever calling `resource.setType(...)`; only the single blanket/catch-all resource created in init() has its type explicitly set (`resource.setType(type)`). Because of this, individually-created per-client resources (e.g. the resource representing a single client granted MANAGE/VIEW) are not tagged with type "Clients" and will not be returned by findByType, so getClientsWithPermission will under-report clients that only have an individual (non-blanket) permission grant. There is also no test in this PR that exercises getClientsWithPermission with a per-client (non-'all') grant, so this gap would not be caught by CI.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.

false_positives.candidate:

The new helper `isAccessTokenId(String expectedGrantShortcut)` is supposed to verify that the grant-type shortcut encoded in the access token id matches the expected grant. Two bugs make this check ineffective:
1. Wrong offset: the encoded context is laid out as sessionType(2 chars) + tokenType(2 chars) + grantType(2 chars), so the grant shortcut occupies index 4-6, but the code extracts `items[0].substring(3, 5)`, which actually reads the last char of the tokenType plus the first char of the grantType – never the real grant shortcut.
2. Inverted logic: even if the offset were correct, the code does `if (... .equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` – i.e. it treats a *matching* shortcut as a failed match, and anything that does NOT match falls through to `return isUUID().matches(items[1])`, which ignores the grant check entirely.

Arroyo's StreamProcessor calls close()/join() on the current strategy on every partition revoke (which happens on every consumer-group rebalance, e.g. deploys/scaling) before calling create_with_partitions() again for the new assignment. Since the pool is never recreated, the new strategy instance submits work into queues that have already been shut down. In FixedQueuePool.submit(), add_offset() runs before work_queue.put(); when put() then fails against the shut-down queue, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()'s except branch calls add_offset()+complete_offset() again, marking the offset as processed even though the message was never handed to a worker. The periodic commit loop then commits these offsets. The net effect is that after the very first rebalance, the consumer silently stops doing any real work while continuing to advance/commit offsets, i.e. permanent, hard-to-notice data loss until logs are inspected.

Combined with WorkItem retaining the full original Message (including raw payload), a single slow group under sustained load will cause unbounded memory growth in that queue instead of applying backpressure, which is exactly the scenario (a slow item clogging processing) this PR claims to address — here it manifests as a potential OOM rather than a batch stall.

This needs to be verified against Sentry's supported Python version; if unsupported, graceful shutdown silently never happens (thread leak and no real teardown).

Instead, any FilteredPayload reaching submit() causes decode_payload to raise AssertionError, which is caught by the generic `except Exception` in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() and logged as 'Error submitting message to queue' even though a filtered payload is an expected, non-error condition. This produces misleading error-level log noise for a normal case and masks real decode errors among the noise.

join(timeout) ignores the supplied timeout and re-runs close() with hard-coded internal timeouts

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(self, timeout=None) simply calls self.close() again, discarding the caller-supplied timeout entirely. close() internally uses fixed 5.0s timeouts for the commit thread join and (via FixedQueuePool.shutdown) for each worker join. This means any operator-configured join timeout (e.g. via the consumer's --join-timeout / join_timeout plumbing in sentry/consumers/__init__.py) has no effect for the thread-queue-parallel mode, and shutdown duration is not actually controlled by the configured value, which can surprise operators expecting a bounded, configurable shutdown.

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts an invariant the implementation does not provide

This test expects that when the first of two same-group messages raises during processing, offsets are not committed (`assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`). However OrderedQueueWorker.run() unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in a `finally` block regardless of whether result_processor raised, so both submitted offsets (100 and 101) become 'complete' and thus committable as soon as the periodic (1s-interval) commit loop runs. Given the test waits up to ~2 seconds for processing/queue-draining before asserting, the commit loop is very likely to have already run and committed by the time the assertion executes, making the assertion either reliably false or flaky depending on timing, rather than verifying a real guarantee.

Test decoder diverges from production decode_payload, masking the FilteredPayload assertion bug

TestSimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.setUp defines a custom `decoder` function that explicitly checks `isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)` and returns None, unlike the actual production decoder (ResultsStrategyFactory.decode_payload) which asserts the payload is NOT a FilteredPayload and raises otherwise (see the separate finding on result_consumer.py). Because none of the added tests exercise SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy with the real decode_payload function against a FilteredPayload input, the mismatch between the declared decoder contract and the actual production implementation is not caught by this test suite.

As soon as this code path is reached (any authorized user supplies a cursor string with a negative offset while `enable_advanced_features=True`), the request will raise an unhandled exception and return a 500 instead of paginated results, making the entire 'advanced pagination' feature non-functional and a self-inflicted DoS vector for whoever can trigger it.

If the same member (identical span payload) exists in both sets being merged — e.g. in the edge case where `parent_span_id == span_id` causes `span_key` to equal `set_key`, or if a span payload is present under more than one bucket due to redirect processing/retries — its score (meant to represent an end timestamp used for both flush-timeout tracking and the new `zpopmin` eviction) gets summed with itself, producing a corrupted, non-timestamp value. No test exercises this changed limit, and the change is unrelated to and undocumented in the PR description, which only discusses buffer eviction.

If any in-flight or backlog Kafka message lacks this field (e.g. during a mixed-version rollout where Relay/producers haven't yet guaranteed this field, or on topic replay of older messages), this raises a `KeyError` that is not handled anywhere in this path, which will fail the whole batch and likely crash/stall the consumer. The PR's stated purpose is "Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert," implemented via `zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua when a segment's sorted set exceeds 1000 members. This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets," but the code on the next line (`self.offset = int(offset)`) is unchanged from before — `int()` already accepted negative numbers. In remove(), `IdentityProviderModel storedIdp = idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias);` is now called unconditionally before the isInvalid(cacheKey) check. Previously, when the cache entry was valid (`isInvalid(cacheKey)==false`), the method only consulted the local cache (`realmCache.getCache().get(cacheKey, ...)`) and never hit the delegate/JPA store in that branch. Now every remove() call performs an extra delegate lookup even when the cached CachedIdentityProvider already holds the needed model (available via `cached.getIdentityProvider()` in the else branch), adding an avoidable database round-trip to every IDP removal.

Inconsistent wrapped vs raw model comparison in login-cache invalidation on update

In update(), `idpById = getById(model.getInternalId())` returns an organization-aware wrapped IdentityProviderModel whose isEnabled() also factors in the linked organization's enabled state (see createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel), while `model` (the second argument passed straight through to registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate) is the raw, unwrapped model from the caller whose isEnabled() reflects only the stored 'enabled' attribute. Because getLoginPredicate() tests ENABLED via isEnabled(), comparing the wrapped 'original' against the raw 'updated' is inconsistent: when the organization is disabled, idpById.isEnabled() can be false even though the stored attribute is true, causing registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate to conclude 'no login-eligibility change' and skip cache invalidation even though the raw 'enabled' attribute genuinely changed. Since the underlying idpDelegate.getForLogin() query filters by the raw stored attribute (not the wrapped value), the cached ID list for getForLogin can become stale and keep referencing an IDP whose real enabled flag changed, violating the documented getForLogin() contract that only enabled/eligible IDPs are returned for callers that don't re-check isEnabled() themselves.

No test covers organization enable/disable or removal affecting the new getForLogin cache

testCacheIDPForLogin only exercises create/update/remove on the IdentityProvider itself to verify cache invalidation of the new getForLogin caches. It never tests disabling/enabling the linked Organization or removing the Organization entirely. This matters because OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean.java was specifically changed in this PR to re-check idp.isEnabled() at render time precisely because toggling an organization's enabled flag does not invalidate the getForLogin ID-list cache. There is no test verifying that disabling an organization correctly excludes its IDPs from login, nor that removing an organization properly invalidates/cleans up the new login caches for its linked IDPs, leaving this behavior unverified.

Login-eligibility logic duplicated between getForLogin() search options and getLoginPredicate()

The default getForLogin() method (lines 165-184) determines login eligibility by building search-option maps (LoginFilter.getLoginSearchOptions() plus explicit ORGANIZATION_ID/BROKER_PUBLIC handling), while the new getLoginPredicate() (lines 252-256) re-implements the same eligibility rules as a Predicate for use purely in cache-invalidation decisions in InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider. These two independent representations of the same business rule must be kept manually in sync; if either is changed in the future without updating the other, the Infinispan cache invalidation logic will silently diverge from the actual query semantics, resulting in stale or incorrect getForLogin() cache results.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing double-check of cache after acquiring write lock

After the first (read-locked) check of entryPointAssetsCache fails (e.g., cache not yet populated or cfg.Env == Dev), the code acquires the write lock at line 48 but never re-checks whether another goroutine already populated the cache while waiting for the lock. As a result, under concurrent initial requests (common right after startup), multiple goroutines can all proceed past the first check, serialize on the write lock, and each redundantly re-read and re-parse assets-manifest.json (or hit the CDN) even though the first goroutine already finished and stored a valid result. This doesn't reintroduce the data race, but it defeats part of the purpose of caching and wastes I/O/CPU under load. A standard fix is to re-check `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` immediately after acquiring the write lock and return early if so.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: an incomplete double-checked locking pattern where the code fails to re-check if the cache was populated by another goroutine after acquiring the write lock.
