Without such a test, a future refactor could silently reintroduce the race with no automated signal.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
Storage.Create failure recorded under legacy metrics instead of storage metrics

In DualWriterMode3.Create, when d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` (line 45) instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. This mislabels a Storage (unified store) failure as a Legacy failure in the dual-writer metrics, corrupting the error-rate dashboards/alerts that distinguish unified-storage health from legacy-storage health. The same mistake is repeated in Update (line 129).

Storage.Update failure recorded under legacy metrics instead of storage metrics

In DualWriterMode3.Update, when d.Storage.Update fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. This duplicates the same mislabeling bug found in Create (line 45): a Storage failure is reported as a Legacy failure, which will skew metrics used to monitor the health of each backend independently.

Async legacy writes derive their timeout context from the request context, which is canceled once the handler returns

Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection (lines 51, 110, 135, 163) each spawn a goroutine that does `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, ...)` using the inbound request `ctx` as the parent. For an HTTP server, the request context is canceled once the handler (ServeHTTP) returns; since these methods return the Storage result to the caller immediately after launching the goroutine (without waiting), the apiserver handler will typically finish and the request context will be canceled shortly afterward — well before the 10 second timeout and often before the legacy write even completes. Because cancellation propagates to the derived timeout context, the "safety measure" asynchronous write to legacy storage can be silently aborted on effectively every request, defeating the purpose of mode 3's async legacy write. The goroutine should detach from request cancellation (e.g. use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` or a fresh context carrying only the needed values) before applying its own timeout.

Legacy write errors are silently swallowed (no logging) in async goroutines

In the async legacy-write goroutines for Create (line 56), Delete (line 113), Update (line 140), and DeleteCollection (line 166), the only outcome recorded on failure is a boolean passed into the duration metric (`d.recordLegacyDuration(errObjectSt != nil, ...)`); none of them call `log.Error(...)` the way the previous Mode3 implementation did (e.g. "could not update object in legacy store"). Operators now have no way to see which object/resource failed to replicate to legacy storage except by correlating metrics, substantially reducing observability for a feature explicitly intended as a safety net against unified-storage/legacy divergence.

Update no longer guarantees the same resolved object is written to both stores

The previous Mode3.Update implementation fetched the current object from Storage, resolved `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)` once, and wrapped the already-resolved object so that both Storage.Update and Legacy.Update applied the exact same final object. The new implementation instead calls `d.Storage.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` and then, in the async goroutine, calls `d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` with the same unresolved `objInfo` (line 139). Each backend will internally invoke `objInfo.UpdatedObject` against its own "old" object; for patch-style updates (merge patch, strategic merge patch, JSON patch) this can produce two different resulting objects if the legacy store's and unified store's current state differ even slightly, causing silent divergence between the two stores — the exact problem dual-writing is meant to prevent. Additionally, invoking `UpdatedObject` a second time may not be safe/idempotent for all `rest.UpdatedObjectInfo` implementations.

TestMode3_Delete never mocks Legacy.Delete even though it is always invoked

DualWriterMode3.Delete unconditionally spawns a goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.Delete(...)` after a successful Storage.Delete. The `testCase` struct in TestMode3_Delete only has a `setupStorageFn` field (no `setupLegacyFn`), so for the "deleting an object in the unified store" success case the legacy mock (`m := &mock.Mock{}`, never associated with `t` via `.Test(t)`) has no registered expectation for `Delete`. Calling an unmocked method on a `testify` mock without `.Test(t)` set panics; since this call happens in a background goroutine, an unrecovered panic there crashes the entire test binary non-deterministically, rather than failing just this test. The test needs to register a Legacy.Delete expectation (and ideally await/verify the call) for success cases.

TestMode3_DeleteCollection never mocks Legacy.DeleteCollection even though it is always invoked

Same issue as in TestMode3_Delete: DualWriterMode3.DeleteCollection always spawns a goroutine calling `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection(...)` after a successful Storage.DeleteCollection, but the `testCase` struct here only defines `setupStorageFn`; there is no `setupLegacyFn` and no `m.On("DeleteCollection", ...)` registered on the legacy mock for the success case. The unmocked call made from the background goroutine will panic in testify's mock (since the mock is not bound to `t`), risking an unrecovered panic that crashes the test process.

No test waits for or verifies the asynchronous legacy write actually occurs

None of the Mode3 tests (Create, Delete, Update, DeleteCollection) synchronize with the goroutine that performs the async legacy write, nor do they call `m.AssertExpectations`/`AssertCalled` to confirm `Legacy.*` was actually invoked. Since the goroutine may run after the subtest has already returned, the tests effectively never verify the core new behavior this PR introduces (asynchronous write-through to legacy storage as a safety measure); a regression that removed the legacy write entirely would not be caught by this test suite.

false_positives.candidate:
Interpolating queries before the $__range exclusion check breaks splitting-safety for $__range queries

In runSplitQuery(), queries are now interpolated via datasource.applyTemplateVariables() (line 299) before being passed to querySupportsSplitting()/isQueryWithRangeVariable() (lines 282-289, used at line 300). isQueryWithRangeVariable() is a textual check for the literal `$__range` placeholder in query.expr. Because interpolation now runs first, any `$__range` usage is already replaced with a concrete value (computed for the original, un-split overall range) before this check executes, so the literal text is gone and isQueryWithRangeVariable() will always return false post-interpolation. As a result, queries that use `$__range` - which the code comment explicitly says must be excluded from time splitting because the backend would otherwise interpolate the range variable using each split sub-range - are no longer routed into `nonSplittingQueries`. Instead they are split normally, and every sub-request ends up reusing the single baked-in value computed for the full original range (e.g. a 3-day range baked into `[3d]`) even though each sub-request only covers a fraction of that range (e.g. 1 day). This silently produces incorrect query results (wrong window/rate calculations) for any metric/log query relying on `$__range`, and effectively makes the exclusion logic in querySupportsSplitting() dead code.

applyTemplateVariables is now invoked redundantly multiple times for the same query in the shard-splitting path

runShardSplitQuery() interpolates all targets via datasource.applyTemplateVariables() (line 52) before delegating to splitQueriesByStreamShard(), which for every shard group/cycle calls runSplitQuery() (querySplitting.ts line 163-166) - and runSplitQuery() itself now also calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables() on its targets (querySplitting.ts line 299). The already-interpolated query is therefore re-interpolated once more for every sub-request that the sharding loop produces. This is confirmed by the updated test in shardQuerySplitting.test.ts (line 112), which now expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times for a single input query (1 initial call + 4 sub-request calls) instead of once as before. Besides the unnecessary repeated work, this is risky if applyTemplateVariables is not fully idempotent (e.g. if it injects ad-hoc filters into the expr string), since re-running it on an already-processed query could duplicate ad-hoc filter matchers or otherwise produce different results depending on context (scopedVars/time range) available at each call site.

No regression test for $__range queries after moving interpolation earlier

The new 'Interpolates queries before execution' test only exercises variable interpolation for `$__auto` and `$step`, which are unrelated to time-range splitting decisions. There is no test verifying that queries containing `$__range` are still excluded from time splitting (routed to nonSplittingQueries) after interpolation now runs before the querySupportsSplitting/isQueryWithRangeVariable check. `.topic-map h3` previously used `color: scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%)`. The new code is `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%))`. The sibling `.map .number, i` rule in the same file correctly kept its original 20% value and used 80% for the counterpart (`dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, 20%), scale-color($secondary, 80%))`), showing the intended pattern. This h3 rule instead was changed to 50%/50%, meaning the light theme's heading color shifts from a dark 20%-lightness shade to a medium 50%-lightness shade, an unintended visual regression.

Lightness value changed (30% -> 50%) in .group-member-info .name, altering light-theme appearance (duplicate of desktop/user.scss issue)

`.user-stream .group-member-info .name` previously used `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`. The new code is `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%))` instead of the expected `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, 30%), scale-color($secondary, 70%))`. This duplicates the same regression found in the desktop variant of this stylesheet: the light theme's text color changes from darker 30%-lightness to lighter 50%-lightness, an unintended side effect beyond the PR's stated scope.

Missed conversion: .topic-list.categories .category .badge-notification color still uses raw scale-color($primary) without a dark-theme fallback

In `.topic-list.categories .category .badge-notification`, `color: scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%);` was left unconverted, while every other occurrence of `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%)` in this same file (e.g. the `th`, `td`, `.topic-excerpt`, and `div.education` rules a few lines above/below) was updated to `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, 50%), scale-color($secondary, 50%))`. Because this instance was missed, the badge-notification text color inside category topic lists will still be computed purely from `$primary` and will not adapt for dark themes, defeating the purpose of this PR for this specific element and likely resulting in poor contrast/readability in dark themes.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the next action, capping the next offset at user_count can produce an empty page (e.g., total equal to limit results in offset == total, showing 2/2 with no members). This can cause confusing UX on the last page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Off-by-one error in totalPages computation causes a phantom empty last page

`totalPages` is computed as `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`. When `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit` (e.g. 100 members with limit 50), this yields 3 instead of the correct 2 pages. Combined with the `next` action's offset calculation (`Math.min(offset + limit, user_count)`), a user can click 'next' from the real last page and land on an extra page whose offset equals `user_count`, which returns zero members from the server (since valid offsets are `0..user_count-1`). The pager will show e.g. 'Page 3/3' with no members listed, and `showingLast` never becomes true until this phantom page is reached. The correct formula should be `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same off-by-one pagination bug where clicking 'next' when total is a multiple of limit (or equal to limit) caps the offset at `user_count`, resulting in a phantom empty last page with no members.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. For example, with 100 users and a limit of 50, it reports 3 pages instead of 2, allowing navigation to an empty page.

The pager will show e.g. 'Page 3/3' with no members listed, and `showingLast` never becomes true until this phantom page is reached. The correct formula should be `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)`.

false_positives.candidate:
Breaking change to /groups/:id/members.json response shape and default page size

The `members` action used to return a plain serialized array for non-automatic groups (unbounded) and only paginated automatic groups at a default limit of 200. It now always returns a hash `{members: [...], meta: {total, limit, offset}}` and defaults to a limit of 50 for every group, automatic or not. Any existing API consumer (mobile apps, external integrations, scripts) that expects the previous array response or expects to receive the full membership list for non-automatic groups will break or silently receive only the first 50 members with no indication that pagination occurred. This is a backward-incompatible API change that is not called out or versioned.

No upper bound on client-supplied limit and no validation of offset for /groups/:id/members.json

`limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` and `offset = params[:offset].to_i` are used directly in the query with no maximum cap or minimum validation. A client can request an arbitrarily large `limit` to retrieve an entire (potentially huge, e.g. 'everyone') group's membership in a single request, defeating the purpose of pagination and risking excessive serialization/DB load. A negative `offset` is also not guarded against, which can produce unexpected SQL (Postgres rejects negative OFFSET values), leading to a 500 error for malformed input on this public, non-admin endpoint.

Membership mutation is persisted before the subsequent save-based success/failure check

In `add_members`, `group.add(user)` is called in a loop (which persists the association immediately via the has_many collection), and only afterward is `group.save` checked to decide whether to render success or `render_json_error`. The same pattern exists in `remove_member` with `group.users.delete(user_id)` followed by `group.save`. If `group.save` fails for any unrelated reason (e.g. a validation on the group model), the membership change has already been committed to the database, yet the client is told the operation failed via `render_json_error`, producing an inconsistent/misleading response relative to the actual state of the data.

No spec coverage added for the rewritten /groups/:id/members pagination behavior

The `members` action was substantially rewritten: response shape changed to `{members:, meta:}`, pagination now applies uniformly to automatic and non-automatic groups, and the default limit changed from effectively unlimited (non-automatic) / 200 (automatic) to 50 for all groups. No corresponding spec file (e.g. groups_controller_spec.rb) was added or updated in this PR to verify the new `meta` payload, default/overridden limit and offset behavior, or the total count, leaving this behavior-changing rewrite untested.

addMembers/removeMember actions silently swallow AJAX failures

Unlike `save` and `destroy`, which attach failure handlers that show a `bootbox.alert` with the server error, the `removeMember` and `addMembers` actions call `this.get('model').removeMember(member)` / `addMembers(usernames)` without attaching any rejection handler. If the request fails (e.g. a 422 for an automatic group, or a network error), the promise rejection is unhandled and the admin receives no feedback that the action did not take effect. Additionally the `addMembers` action leaves a `// TODO: should clear the input` comment, meaning the username input is never cleared after a successful add, which can lead to accidental duplicate submissions.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BlockedEmail match_count/last_match_at are double-counted per signup attempt

In UsersController#create, `user.valid?` is called explicitly (line 168) and then `user.save` is called again a few lines later (line 172). Rails reruns all validations on every call to valid?/save, so the new EmailValidator (and therefore BlockedEmail.should_block?, which mutates and saves the matched BlockedEmail row) executes twice per request. This means `match_count` is incremented by 2 instead of 1 and `last_match_at`/the extra `BlockedEmail` lookup+save happen twice for every single signup attempt (not just discourse-hub flows, since `user.valid?` is evaluated unconditionally due to `&&` short-circuit order). This corrupts the statistics the feature is meant to produce and doubles the DB load added by this feature on every signup.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same underlying design flaw: the predicate method `BlockedEmail.should_block_email?` (or `should_block?`) has side effects that mutate and save statistics (`match_count`, `last_match_at`) during a read/validation check. The candidate issue takes this a step further by explaining the concrete bug this causes in Rails (validations running twice during `valid?` and `save`, leading to double-counting), while the golden comment frames it as a general command-query separation and concurrency concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive, allowing trivial bypass

`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` performs an exact, case-sensitive string match against the stored email. Since email addresses are effectively case-insensitive, a spammer whose address was blocked (e.g. `spam@example.com`) can bypass the block entirely simply by submitting `Spam@Example.com` or any other casing variant. This defeats the purpose of the feature. The whitelist/blacklist domain check in lib/validators/email_validator.rb uses a case-insensitive regex, but the new block-list lookup does not normalize case at all.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same vulnerability: the email lookup in `BlockedEmail` is case-sensitive, which allows blocked users to bypass the check by changing the casing of their email address.

false_positives.candidate:
Non-atomic read-modify-write race on match_count

should_block? loads the BlockedEmail row, increments `match_count` in Ruby, then calls `save`. Two concurrent signup requests for the same blocked email can both read the same `match_count` value before either writes back, so one increment is silently lost (classic lost-update race). The statistic is also not updated atomically with respect to `last_match_at`. This should use an atomic DB update (e.g. `update_counters`, `increment!`, or a raw SQL `UPDATE ... SET match_count = match_count + 1`) instead of a load-then-save round trip.

rejectedEmails array is a shared mutable default shared across controller instances

`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is declared as a plain property value in `.extend()`, so this exact array object is evaluated once at class-definition time and shared by the prototype. `createAccount` later calls `pushObject` on it (line 275), mutating the shared array in place. Any new instance of CreateAccountController created later (e.g. if the modal controller is re-instantiated) will see emails rejected by a completely unrelated prior session/instance, incorrectly failing emailValidation for emails that were never rejected for that instance. The array should be initialized per-instance in an `init()` hook instead of as a literal default value.

No end-to-end test for blocked-email signup rejection or new response fields

The create action now returns `errors` and `values` fields on failure specifically to support the new client-side rejectedEmails tracking, and signups are expected to be rejected when the submitted email matches a BlockedEmail record. There is no request/controller spec asserting that POST /users with a blocked email is rejected and that the JSON response includes the `errors`/`values` keys the JS controller depends on. Only the isolated EmailValidator and BlockedEmail model specs exist, so the full integration path (controller -> User#valid? -> EmailValidator -> BlockedEmail) is untested.

EmailValidator spec omits whitelist/blacklist coverage removed from User model

The domain whitelist/blacklist validation logic previously lived in User#email_validator/email_in_restriction_setting? and is now moved into EmailValidator (lib/validators/email_validator.rb), but this new spec file only exercises the 'blocked email' branch. There is no test verifying `email_domains_whitelist`/`email_domains_blacklist` behavior still works correctly after being relocated out of user.rb, leaving that previously-tested logic without direct validator-level coverage.

New rejectedEmails client logic has no test coverage

The new rejectedEmails tracking in emailValidation (lines 69-74) and the pushObject call in createAccount (lines 274-276) introduce new client-visible behavior that gates form submission, but no JS unit test was added to verify that a rejected email correctly fails emailValidation/submitDisabled or that successful resubmission with a different email clears the failure.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`.panel`'s new flex alignment (`margin-left:auto`, `order(3)`) only works if it is a direct child of the flex container `.contents`

`.panel` previously used `float: right;` to sit at the right edge of the header regardless of exact DOM nesting depth. It now relies on `margin-left: auto;` plus `@include order(3);` (lines 36-39), both of which only affect direct flex-item children of a flex container — here `.contents` (line 14-19), which is the only selector given `display:flex`. The SCSS itself declares `.panel` as a sibling rule under `.d-header`, not nested inside `.contents`, so whether this works depends entirely on the actual HTML template making `.panel` a direct child of the `.contents` element — something not verifiable from this diff and not covered by any test or screenshot. If that assumption is wrong, the panel (containing search/user menu/hamburger) will fall into normal block flow and break the header layout instead of being right-aligned.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same core problem: replacing `float: right` on `.d-header .panel` with flexbox properties (`margin-left: auto` and `order`) will break right-alignment if `.panel` is not a direct child of the flex container (`.contents`), causing it to fall back to normal block flow and stack instead of aligning right.

false_positives.candidate:
Float-based children lose intended layout once `.small-action` becomes a flex container

`.small-action` now has `@include flexbox();` (display:flex) added, but its children `.topic-avatar` (line 270, `float: left;`) and `button` (line 309, `float: right;`) still rely on CSS floats. Per the flexbox spec, float/clear have no effect on flex items, so these children become ordinary flex items laid out in document order (avatar, description, button) instead of being pushed to opposite edges as before. The dismiss/undo button that previously sat flush right via `float: right` will now simply follow the description text in the flex row, changing its visual position in every 'small action' post entry (e.g. 'topic closed by...') without any compensating `margin-left: auto` or `order` rule being added.

Unrelated spacing changes bundled into a 'flexbox mixin' PR without explanation

Alongside the stated goal of introducing flexbox mixins, this file also changes `.small-action-desc` padding from `0.5em 0 0.5em 4em` to `0 1.5%` (line 280), removes `margin-top: 5px` on the same rule, changes `.custom-message p` margin from `5px 0` to `0` (around line 292), and removes `padding-top: 4px` from `.small-action-desc > p` (previously present, now removed). These are independent visual/spacing regressions unrelated to adding flexbox mixins, with no rationale given in the PR description, making it hard to verify whether the removal of the left-padding offset (which compensated for the floated avatar icon width) still renders correctly for all 'small action' message variants.

Removed bullet-badge vertical offset without replacement, risking misalignment

The diff removes `&.bullet { margin-top: 5px; }` from inside `.extra-info-wrapper .badge-wrapper` while only adding `@include order(2);` and `line-height: 1.5;` to the parent `.extra-info-wrapper`. This margin-top was presumably tuned to vertically align the bullet-style category badge (rendered with `inline-flex`/`align-items: baseline` in badges.css.scss) with surrounding text. Removing it with no compensating adjustment can reintroduce the vertical misalignment it was originally added to fix, and the change is unrelated to the stated purpose of adding flexbox mixins.

PR title/description mischaracterizes the change as a 'performance optimization' with no supporting rationale

The PR title claims to 'Optimize header layout performance with flexbox mixins,' but the actual change only replaces/adds cross-browser vendor-prefixed flexbox declarations (display, align-items, order) and refactors some raw CSS into mixins; no performance measurement, profiling, or reasoning is provided to support a performance claim. Meanwhile, the PR description is just 'Test 5', giving reviewers no information about why several unrelated spacing/margin changes (header .panel/.title, topic small-action spacing, badge margins) were bundled in, nor any confirmation that visual regression/manual testing was performed across browsers for these cross-cutting CSS changes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is missing the trailing '?' required by the serializer convention

Every other conditional attribute in this file follows the `include_#{attr}?` naming convention (e.g. `include_email?`, `include_card_image_badge_id?`, and the dynamically generated `include_#{attr}?` methods from `staff_attributes`/`private_attributes`/`untrusted_attributes`). The new method is defined as `def include_website_name` (no `?`), so the serializer will never find/call it as the inclusion-guard for the `website_name` attribute. As a result `website_name` is unconditionally included in the serialized output (even as `null` when `website` is blank), ignoring the intended `website.present?` gate. This also means any attempt to hide `website_name` based on trust-level/anonymous rules (see related finding) cannot work even if added, since the guard method itself is never invoked.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the main bug described in the golden comment: the `include_website_name` method is missing the trailing `?` required by the serializer convention for conditional attribute inclusion. Although the golden comment also mentions a secondary issue regarding string concatenation, the core bug is clearly matched.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name leaks the restricted website attribute to untrusted/anonymous viewers

`website` is listed in `untrusted_attributes` (lines 105-111), which hides it from anonymous viewers when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` is true (e.g. TL0 users). The new derived attribute `website_name` (lines 137-155) is computed directly from `website` via `object.user_profile.website` but is not added to `untrusted_attributes` and has no equivalent restriction check (its `include_website_name` method only checks `website.present?`, not the trust/anonymous restriction). Consequently, a TL0 user's website hostname (and sometimes the full host+path) will still be exposed to anonymous visitors even though the underlying `website` field is correctly hidden for them, defeating the existing privacy control.

No test verifying website_name is restricted for TL0/anonymous viewers like website

The 'with a TL0 user seen as anonymous' context (lines 6-16) asserts that `website` and other untrusted attributes are hidden, but does not include `website_name` in `untrusted_attributes` nor set a website on the fabricated user to actually exercise the check. This missing coverage allowed the access-control gap (website_name leaking despite website being restricted) and the broken `include_website_name` guard to go unnoticed.

Asymmetric subdomain matching logic in website_name

The matching logic handles the case where the Discourse host has an extra subdomain relative to the website host (e.g. website 'example.com' vs instance 'forums.example.com', tested in spec), via `discourse_host.ends_with?("." << website_host)`. However the reverse case — the website host has an extra subdomain relative to a bare instance domain (e.g. website 'http://forum.example.com' vs instance host 'example.com') — is not handled: the `ends_with?` check is only performed in one direction, so this case falls through without expanding to the full path even though it represents the same underlying domain relationship. This asymmetry is untested and likely not intended given the feature's goal of detecting same-domain websites.

Mutating string literal with << instead of safe concatenation

`discourse_host.ends_with?("." << website_host)` uses the mutating `<<` operator on the string literal `"."` rather than `+` or interpolation. This happens to work today because the file has no `# frozen_string_literal: true` magic comment, but it is fragile: if frozen string literals are enabled for this file in the future (a common Rails convention), this line will raise a `FrozenError` at runtime. It should use `".#{website_host}"` or `"." + website_host` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring match instead of exact comparison

`postMessageReceived` validates the message sender with `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1`. This checks whether `e.origin` occurs anywhere inside `discourseUrl` rather than requiring an exact origin match. A malicious page whose origin happens to be a prefix (or other substring) of the configured `discourseUrl` string would pass this check and be able to send fake `discourse-resize` messages (and any future message types added to this handler) to the embedding page. The check should compare `e.origin` against the expected origin with strict equality rather than `indexOf`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same vulnerability: the origin validation using `indexOf` on `discourseUrl` and `e.origin` performs a substring match instead of an exact origin check, allowing malicious origins to bypass the check.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Invalid Ruby syntax `end if` breaks the embed view

The template closes the `if/else` block with `<%- end if %>` instead of `<%- end %>`. `end if` with no condition after `if` is not valid Ruby (the `if` keyword here has nothing to modify/condition on), so this template will raise a SyntaxError (wrapped in ActionView::Template::Error) whenever it is compiled/rendered. Since this view is rendered whenever `EmbedController#best` finds an existing `topic_id`, the core feature of this PR (showing embedded discourse comments) will 500 for every successful request. This should simply be `<%- end %>`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same syntax error in the ERB template: closing an `if` block with `end if` instead of `end`, which causes a syntax error at render time.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feed item content assumed always present; no test for malformed/short items

`content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes every RSS/Atom item exposes a non-nil `content` (e.g. `content:encoded`). Plain RSS 2.0 feeds frequently only provide `description`, in which case `i.content` can be `nil`, causing `nil.scrub` to raise `NoMethodError` and fail the whole scheduled job (no items get imported, not just the bad one). There is no test exercising `poll_feed` itself (spec/jobs/poll_feed_spec.rb only tests the guard conditions in `execute`), so this failure mode is untested and unguarded.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: calling `i.content.scrub` assumes `i.content` is non-nil, which will cause a nil error/NoMethodError on RSS feeds that only provide a `description` field instead of `content`.

false_positives.candidate:
absolutize_urls mangles protocol-relative URLs

`absolutize_urls` treats any `href`/`src` starting with `/` as site-relative and rewrites it by stripping all leading slashes and prepending `prefix + "/"`. Protocol-relative URLs such as `//cdn.example.com/image.png` also start with `/`, so `href.sub(/^\/+/, '')` strips both leading slashes, turning the URL into `cdn.example.com/image.png`, which then becomes `prefix/cdn.example.com/image.png` (e.g. `http://eviltrout.com/cdn.example.com/image.png`) — a broken link to the wrong host instead of the intended absolute external resource. This affects both the `a['href']` and `img['src']` rewriting blocks (lines ~62-73).

raw_html cook method bypasses sanitization for externally-sourced content

`Post#cook` now returns `raw` verbatim (skipping `PrettyText`/`post_analyzer.cook`) when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. This mode is used for all posts created via `TopicEmbed.import` (app/models/topic_embed.rb line 22), including content pulled from `app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb`, which feeds raw RSS/Atom `content` (only `CGI.unescapeHTML`'d, never sanitized) directly into `TopicEmbed.import`. The resulting `cooked` value is later rendered unescaped via `<%= raw post.cooked %>` in app/views/embed/best.html.erb. If the configured feed (or a compromised/hijacked feed source) contains `<script>` or other malicious markup, it will be served verbatim to all visitors of the embed page, bypassing Discourse's normal HTML sanitization pipeline entirely — a stored XSS risk.

Race condition can raise unhandled uniqueness violation in TopicEmbed.import

When `embed.blank?` is true, a new Topic/Post/TopicEmbed is created. Two concurrent calls to `import` for the same new `embed_url` (e.g. two users hitting the embed controller at the same time before any embed exists) can both see `embed.blank? == true` and both attempt `TopicEmbed.create!(embed_url: url, ...)`. The unique index on `embed_url` (migration 20131217174004) will reject the second insert, but there is no rescue for `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique`/`StatementInvalid`, so the second caller's `TopicRetriever`/background job will raise an unhandled exception instead of gracefully reusing the already-created embed.

Disqus import tool silently drops the --category option

The previous implementation accepted `-c/--category` to assign imported Disqus threads to a specific category and passed `category: category_id` into `PostCreator.new`. The new implementation calls `TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], title: t[:title])`, which has no way to specify a category, and the `method_option :category` declaration itself was removed. Any existing script or documentation relying on `thor disqus:import -c <category>` will now silently ignore the option (or error, since the option no longer exists), a backward-incompatible regression with no migration note.

Test does not stub TopicView.new's return value

`TopicEmbed.expects(:topic_id_for_embed).returns(123)` and `TopicView.expects(:new).with(123, nil, {best: 5})` mock `TopicView.new` without a `.returns(...)`, so it returns `nil` by default. The controller then sets `@topic_view = nil` and implicitly renders `best.html.erb`, which calls `@topic_view.posts.present?` — this will raise `NoMethodError` on `nil`, so the subsequent `after` block assertion (`response.should be_success`) can never be reached; the test will error rather than pass/fail meaningfully, meaning the 'creates a topic view when a topic_id is found' path is not actually verified to render correctly.

Same cache duration applied to loading and completed states

`discourse_expires_in 1.minute` is called unconditionally for both the "loading" (topic not yet retrieved) and "found" (topic_view rendered) branches. false_positives.candidate:
New SpansBuffer instance created on every process restart without cleaning up the old one

`_create_process_for_shards` (called both on initial startup and from `_ensure_processes_alive` on every restart, e.g. line 259) always constructs a brand-new `SpansBuffer(shards)` and overwrites `self.buffers[process_index]` (line 125). Previously, a single buffer object was created once in `__init__` and reused across restarts. Now, every unhealthy-process restart creates a fresh buffer/Redis client without explicitly closing the previous one, which can leak Redis connections over the lifetime of a long-running consumer that experiences repeated flusher process restarts.

Memory backpressure check now aggregates memory info across per-process sub-buffers, risking double counting

`submit()` now iterates `self.buffers.values()` (one `SpansBuffer` per flusher-process shard group, each created independently via `SpansBuffer(shards)`) and sums `get_memory_info()` results across them (lines 299-303), instead of calling `get_memory_info()` once on a single buffer covering all assigned shards as before. If `get_memory_info()` reports memory per underlying Redis host rather than per shard, and two different process groups contain shards that map to the same physical Redis host, that host's memory will be counted multiple times in the aggregated `used`/`available` sum. This directly feeds the `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` hard-backpressure check used to avoid Redis OOM, so an incorrect aggregation could cause the check to behave incorrectly (false positive or negative backpressure).

Dead/unused method `_create_process_for_shard`

`_create_process_for_shard` (singular, lines 127-132) is defined to look up the process group for a single shard and restart it, but it is never called anywhere in the class — `_ensure_processes_alive` calls `_create_process_for_shards` (plural) directly with the already-known shard list. This leaves dead code in place, suggesting either an incomplete refactor or a helper that should have been used instead of duplicating the lookup logic.

New --flusher-processes option defaults to 1, disabling the new multi-process-per-shard behavior by default

The new `--flusher-processes` CLI option defaults to `1`. As a result, the headline feature of this PR (spawning one flusher process per Redis shard) is not enabled unless operators explicitly override this CLI flag in deployment configuration — worth calling out since the PR description implies this is the new default behavior.

Given this PR substantially rewrote the restart logic to be per-process-group instead of global, this is an important gap in test coverage for a concurrency-sensitive code path.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BuildIndex no longer serializes concurrent builds for the same key

The previous implementation locked cacheMu for the entire BuildIndex call, which (while slow) also serialized concurrent build attempts for the same NamespacedResource key. Now the lock only protects the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write. getOrCreateIndex() in search.go has no locking either (it just checks GetIndex() for nil and calls build() if so), so two concurrent calls for the same cold key (e.g. two simultaneous Search requests, or a Search racing with a watch event) can both perform a full BuildIndex, each creating its own bleve.Index (including on-disk files for file-backed indexes), and whichever finishes last silently overwrites b.cache[key]; the loser's index/resources are never closed or cleaned up, leaking file handles/disk usage and duplicating work.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: moving cacheMu locking from the entire BuildIndex operation to only the final cache assignment allows concurrent goroutines to build the same expensive index for the same key. The candidate adds potential resource-leak consequences without changing the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs() reads cache map without holding cacheMu, racing with BuildIndex writes

TotalDocs() iterates over b.cache with `for _, v := range b.cache` without acquiring cacheMu (neither RLock nor Lock), while BuildIndex now writes to the same map under cacheMu.Lock() after doing the (now unlocked) expensive build work concurrently. Since BuildIndex calls can run concurrently for different keys (that is the whole point of this PR's locking change) and TotalDocs can be invoked at the same time (e.g. the search.go init() logging call right after group.Wait(), or any external caller/metrics path), this is an unsynchronized concurrent map read/write. Go maps are not safe for concurrent read/write; this can produce a 'fatal error: concurrent map read and map write' crash, not just a benign race. GetIndex already correctly uses RLock for cache reads; TotalDocs should do the same.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same unsynchronized access to b.cache: TotalDocs iterates the map while concurrent BuildIndex calls can write to it, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic. The candidate also references the initialization logging call highlighted by the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
NewResourceServer now blocks synchronously on full index build

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) before returning, and Init() runs the full search index build for every namespace (searchSupport.init). Previously NewResourceServer returned immediately and Init() was deferred to the first gRPC call. Index building can take a long time (this is exactly the problem the PR is trying to avoid inside gRPC request contexts), so now the constructor itself can block for an arbitrarily long time, and will fail outright (returning nil, err) if anything in Init fails. Any caller of NewResourceServer that expects a cheap/fast constructor (process startup with readiness/liveness timeouts, module startup sequencing, tests) can now time out or fail to start. The PR description itself asks 'what could this break?' which indicates this tradeoff was not fully evaluated; no caller-side timeout/async handling was added to accommodate the new blocking behavior.

Parallel index build goroutines race on shared err and counter variables

In searchSupport.init(), the errgroup loop spawns one goroutine per namespace (group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers) allows real concurrency) and each goroutine does `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...); return err`, where both `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` are variables captured from the enclosing scope and written concurrently by multiple goroutines without any mutex/atomic. This is a data race: concurrent non-atomic increments of totalBatchesIndexed can lose updates, and concurrent writes to the shared `err` mean a goroutine's `return err` can read a value written by a different goroutine between assignment and return, causing errgroup to receive an incorrect per-goroutine result (e.g. returning another goroutine's error for a successful build, or masking a real failure with nil from a later successful goroutine). This can cause init() to incorrectly fail startup, or silently swallow a failed index build. Each goroutine should use its own local err variable and totalBatchesIndexed should be an atomic counter or protected by a mutex.

Postgres integration test skipped instead of fixed, masking potential regression

The test now unconditionally skips when dbType == 'postgres' with the comment 'test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.' This removes CI coverage of the storage-server module startup path for Postgres, one of the supported production databases, right in the same PR that changes resource-server initialization to run synchronously and eagerly at construction time. Skipping rather than diagnosing/fixing risks hiding a real regression introduced by the eager-Init change (e.g., startup taking too long or behaving differently under Postgres in CI) and leaves no coverage to catch future regressions on that backend until the TODO is addressed.

Trace-context propagation fix applied inconsistently within the same file

The PR fixes span propagation in GetResourceStats by reassigning `ctx, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` so the span is attached to the context used by the subsequent DB call. However, sibling methods in the same file with the identical bug were left unfixed, e.g. ReadResource (line 353: `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, tracePrefix+".Read")`, followed by `b.db.WithTx(ctx, ...)` using the original, span-less ctx), WriteEvent (line ~158), and ListIterator (line ~388). Since the PR's stated goal is 'fixes trace propagation by passing span contexts down', leaving these other call sites with the same discarded-context pattern means their DB operations still won't appear nested under their respective spans in traces, contradicting the PR's intent and leaving inconsistent tracing behavior in the same backend file.

false_positives.candidate:
close()/terminate() destroy the factory-level shared queue pool, breaking processing after every rebalance

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() and terminate() call self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which shuts down every worker thread and all underlying queues. However, FixedQueuePool is created exactly once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ (result_consumer.py) and is reused unchanged across every subsequent create_with_partitions() call (create_thread_queue_parallel_worker just returns a new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy wrapping the same self.queue_pool). Arroyo's StreamProcessor calls close()/join() on the current strategy on every partition revoke (which happens on every consumer-group rebalance, e.g. deploys/scaling) before calling create_with_partitions() again for the new assignment. Since the pool is never recreated, the new strategy instance submits work into queues that have already been shut down. In FixedQueuePool.submit(), add_offset() runs before work_queue.put(); when put() then fails against the shut-down queue, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()'s except branch calls add_offset()+complete_offset() again, marking the offset as processed even though the message was never handed to a worker. The periodic commit loop then commits these offsets. The net effect is that after the very first rebalance, the consumer silently stops doing any real work while continuing to advance/commit offsets, i.e. permanent, hard-to-notice data loss until logs are inspected.

Worker queues are unbounded, so there is no actual backpressure

Each per-queue work_queue is created with queue.Queue() (no maxsize), so put() never blocks. The class docstring for SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy explicitly claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but there is nothing enforcing that: submit() is always non-blocking regardless of how backlogged a given group's queue is. Combined with WorkItem retaining the full original Message (including raw payload), a single slow group under sustained load will cause unbounded memory growth in that queue instead of applying backpressure, which is exactly the scenario (a slow item clogging processing) this PR claims to address — here it manifests as a potential OOM rather than a batch stall.

Reliance on queue.Queue.shutdown()/queue.ShutDown, which require Python 3.13+

queue.Queue.shutdown() and the queue.ShutDown exception were only added to the standard library in Python 3.13. If the deployed runtime is on an older Python version, q.shutdown(immediate=False) raises AttributeError, which is swallowed by the surrounding `except Exception: logger.exception(...)` in FixedQueuePool.shutdown() (lines 236-240). Because this is the only mechanism used to interrupt the blocking self.work_queue.get() call in OrderedQueueWorker.run() (lines 131-133), the worker threads never actually unblock when the AttributeError path is hit, so they keep running (or block forever) despite shutdown() ostensibly having completed. This needs to be verified against Sentry's supported Python version; if unsupported, graceful shutdown silently never happens (thread leak and no real teardown).

Worker shutdown joins threads sequentially, so shutdown time scales with num_queues

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() joins each worker thread sequentially with a 5 second timeout per worker (`for worker in self.workers: worker.join(timeout=5.0)`). With the default of 20 queues/workers, if workers are stuck (e.g. due to the queue.Queue.shutdown compatibility issue noted elsewhere, or simply slow in-flight processing), this loop can take up to num_queues * 5 seconds (100s by default) to return, rather than a bounded ~5s. This can make consumer shutdown unexpectedly slow and risks the process being force-killed by orchestration before a graceful stop completes.

decode_payload asserts against FilteredPayload, but the queue strategy's decoder contract requires handling it

decode_payload has `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)`. create_thread_queue_parallel_worker passes `partial(self.decode_payload, self.topic_for_codec)` as the `decoder` for SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy, whose declared type is `Callable[[KafkaPayload | FilteredPayload], T | None]` — i.e. it is expected to tolerate FilteredPayload inputs and return None. Instead, any FilteredPayload reaching submit() causes decode_payload to raise AssertionError, which is caught by the generic `except Exception` in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() and logged as 'Error submitting message to queue' even though a filtered payload is an expected, non-error condition. This produces misleading error-level log noise for a normal case and masks real decode errors among the noise.

join(timeout) ignores the supplied timeout and re-runs close() with hard-coded internal timeouts

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(self, timeout=None) simply calls self.close() again, discarding the caller-supplied timeout entirely. close() internally uses fixed 5.0s timeouts for the commit thread join and (via FixedQueuePool.shutdown) for each worker join. This means any operator-configured join timeout (e.g. via the consumer's --join-timeout / join_timeout plumbing in sentry/consumers/__init__.py) has no effect for the thread-queue-parallel mode, and shutdown duration is not actually controlled by the configured value, which can surprise operators expecting a bounded, configurable shutdown.

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts an invariant the implementation does not provide

This test expects that when the first of two same-group messages raises during processing, offsets are not committed (`assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`). However OrderedQueueWorker.run() unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in a `finally` block regardless of whether result_processor raised, so both submitted offsets (100 and 101) become 'complete' and thus committable as soon as the periodic (1s-interval) commit loop runs. Given the test waits up to ~2 seconds for processing/queue-draining before asserting, the commit loop is very likely to have already run and committed by the time the assertion executes, making the assertion either reliably false or flaky depending on timing, rather than verifying a real guarantee.

Test decoder diverges from production decode_payload, masking the FilteredPayload assertion bug

TestSimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.setUp defines a custom `decoder` function that explicitly checks `isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)` and returns None, unlike the actual production decoder (ResultsStrategyFactory.decode_payload) which asserts the payload is NOT a FilteredPayload and raises otherwise (see the separate finding on result_consumer.py). Because none of the added tests exercise SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy with the real decode_payload function against a FilteredPayload input, the mismatch between the declared decoder contract and the actual production implementation is not caught by this test suite.

The comment claiming "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is incorrect. As soon as this code path is reached (any authorized user supplies a cursor string with a negative offset while `enable_advanced_features=True`), the request will raise an unhandled exception and return a 500 instead of paginated results, making the entire 'advanced pagination' feature non-functional and a self-inflicted DoS vector for whoever can trigger it.

Its explanation of Django rejecting negative indices describes the consequence of that same issue.

true_positives.matched_candidate:

This only guards the forward-pagination case; when `cursor.is_prev` is True, the raw (potentially negative, since `Cursor.offset` is parsed directly from user-supplied cursor strings via `int(bits[1])`) offset is passed straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, which will raise an exception on Django querysets. The fix is incomplete/inconsistent: it protects one pagination direction but leaves the other exposed to the same crash.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in BasePaginator.get_result(): previous-page cursors use the raw offset without clamping, allowing negative values to reach queryset slicing.

false_positives.candidate:
Overly broad authorization gate for a pagination path that crashes

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` allows any organization member with "global access" (not just superusers/admins) to opt into `OptimizedCursorPaginator` via the `optimized_pagination=true` query param. The in-code comments describe this as being for "authorized administrators" only, but `has_global_access` is a much weaker bar than superuser. Combined with the broken negative-offset handling in `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (see paginator.py finding), this means a relatively large set of non-admin users can trigger unhandled 500s on this endpoint just by crafting a cursor string, and the intended admin-only restriction is not actually enforced as described.

After switching the span buffer from Redis sets (`sadd`/`sunionstore`) to sorted sets (`zadd`/`zunionstore`) keyed by `end_timestamp_precise`, the `zunionstore` calls at lines 47 and 53 do not specify `AGGREGATE MIN`, so Redis defaults to `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the same member (identical span payload) exists in both sets being merged — e.g. in the edge case where `parent_span_id == span_id` causes `span_key` to equal `set_key`, or if a span payload is present under more than one bucket due to redirect processing/retries — its score (meant to represent an end timestamp used for both flush-timeout tracking and the new `zpopmin` eviction) gets summed with itself, producing a corrupted, non-timestamp value. This can cause spans to be evicted/retained in the wrong order or to never expire as intended, silently defeating the new eviction logic this PR introduces.

The loop bound for resolving the redirect chain was reduced from `0, 10000` to `0, 1000`, and the previous explanatory comment ("theoretically this limit means segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was removed entirely rather than updated. This silently lowers the maximum depth of a redirect/parent chain that can be correctly resolved before the script gives up, risking incorrect segment joining for deeply-nested span trees that previously worked. No test exercises this changed limit, and the change is unrelated to and undocumented in the PR description, which only discusses buffer eviction.

max_segment_spans parameter is now dead code, and its prior observability was removed without replacement

`SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans` (default 1001), but after this change nothing in `buffer.py` reads `self.max_segment_spans` anymore. Previously, `_load_segment_data` used this value to detect and skip (with `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded")` and an error log) segments whose span count exceeded the limit. That enforcement and its metric were removed in favor of the Lua script's hard-coded eviction at `span_count > 1000`, but no equivalent metric/log was added for the new eviction path, and the now-unused constructor parameter is misleading to callers/tests who may still pass it expecting enforcement.

Eviction cap hardcoded to 1000, decoupled from the Python-configurable (and now-unused) max_segment_spans=1001

The eviction threshold `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000) end` is a magic number baked into the Lua script, no longer driven by the `max_segment_spans` setting on `SpansBuffer` (which is unused after this change, see buffer.py finding). The two numbers (1000 here vs. 1001 previously configured in Python) are also off-by-one from each other, making it easy for future maintainers to believe changing `max_segment_spans` has any effect, when it no longer does.

`process_batch` now does `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` using direct dict indexing (unlike the optional `val.get("parent_span_id")` pattern used elsewhere). If any in-flight or backlog Kafka message lacks this field (e.g. during a mixed-version rollout where Relay/producers haven't yet guaranteed this field, or on topic replay of older messages), this raises a `KeyError` that is not handled anywhere in this path, which will fail the whole batch and likely crash/stall the consumer. This is a behavior change from the previous code which did not require this key at all.

No test coverage for the new >1000-span eviction behavior added by this PR

The PR's stated purpose is "Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert," implemented via `zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua when a segment's sorted set exceeds 1000 members. None of the changes in this test file add a case that inserts more than 1000 spans into a single segment to verify that the oldest entries are correctly evicted, that the retained spans are the newest ones, or that `flush_segments` behaves correctly afterward. The only changes here are adding the new required `end_timestamp_precise` field to existing unrelated test spans, so the core new behavior of this PR is entirely untested.

This PR adds a new paginator class (`OptimizedCursorPaginator`) with a security-relevant negative-offset code path, and wires it into `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` behind a new query parameter and an authorization check. No tests were added for either the paginator class or the new endpoint branch (e.g. verifying authorized vs. unauthorized access, or correct/incorrect handling of negative offsets). Given the broken negative-offset handling identified separately, tests would have caught this before merge.

Misleading comment implies a functional change that doesn't exist in this file

The added comment states "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios... This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets," but the code on the next line (`self.offset = int(offset)`) is unchanged from before — `int()` already accepted negative numbers. No validation or enablement logic was added here. The comment is misleading: it suggests this file deliberately sanctions negative offsets as a safe, supported feature, while the actual consumers of `Cursor.offset` (in paginator.py) do not safely support negative values and will raise exceptions when given one. This can mislead future maintainers into believing negative offsets are a vetted, working feature.

Unrelated, security-sensitive pagination feature bundled into a PR described as a spans-buffer optimization

This PR's title/description describe an optimization to the spans Redis buffer (add-buffer.lua, buffer.py), but it also introduces and wires up an entirely new, broken pagination mechanism (`OptimizedCursorPaginator`, negative-offset cursor handling, and a new `optimized_pagination` endpoint flag in the audit log API) that is unrelated to spans buffering. This combination of an unrelated, under-tested, and crash-prone authorization-adjacent feature with a narrowly-described infra change is the kind of change that should be split into its own PR with explicit review of its authorization model and failure modes; as bundled, it is easy for reviewers focused on the stated spans-buffer change to miss the new attack surface in the pagination code.

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` documents caching the allowlist eligibility result for 60 seconds ("Cache allowlist eligibility for 60 seconds ... eventual consistency is acceptable"), while the helper it calls on a cache miss, `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, states "This function reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time... It should be removed before merge.

The test suite only exercises private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`) but never calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` itself — the function that actually implements the caching behavior described as the PR's core "performance optimization". There is no test validating cache-hit vs cache-miss paths, TTL behavior, or that `invalidate_upsampling_cache` actually clears the correct key. Given the caching logic introduces real correctness risk (stale allowlist decisions, hash-based key collisions), this is the part of the change most in need of direct test coverage, and it currently has none.

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` wraps both the dict traversal (`normalized_data.get("contexts", {}).get("error_sampling", {}).get("client_sample_rate")`) and the float conversion in bare `except Exception: pass` blocks. Any malformed or unexpected shape of `contexts`/`error_sampling` (e.g. `contexts` explicitly set to `None`) will silently skip setting `sample_rate` with no logging or error surfaced, making it harder to diagnose why upsampling-related fixtures in tests produce unexpected counts if the test data doesn't match the expected shape exactly.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key can collide for different (action, name, parent) tuples

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates action, name and parent with a plain '_' delimiter: namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent. Because dashboard/folder UIDs (name, parent) are allowed to contain underscores, two different tuples can produce the exact same string, e.g. (action="dashboards:read", name="a_b", parent="c") and (action="dashboards:read", name="a", parent="b_c") both yield "...perm_<uid>_dashboards:read_a_b_c". Since permDenialCache, permCache, idCache, etc. all share the same underlying cache.Cache instance (only key prefixes differ), this collision causes the cached 'denied' verdict for one resource to be incorrectly applied to a completely different resource/folder combination, producing wrong Check() results for up to the cache TTL.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify ambiguous underscore-delimited concatenation in userPermDenialCacheKey, allowing distinct component tuples to collide and incorrectly reuse cached permission denials. The candidate provides a concrete example of the same underlying bug.

false_positives.candidate:
New denial cache can re-introduce the exact bug this PR fixes via a create/permission-grant race

After a real (non-cached) permission check returns not-allowed, Check() unconditionally stores a 'deny' entry (s.permDenialCache.Set) keyed by namespace/user/action/name/parent, and this entry is consulted first on every subsequent Check() for up to shortCacheTTL (30s), short-circuiting before any DB lookup. If a user creates a resource and the authorization check races with the commit of the resource's permission grant (the exact scenario this PR intends to fix), the first Check() can observe no permission yet, be denied, and have that denial cached for 30 seconds — meaning the creator would be locked out of their own newly created dashboard/folder for up to 30 seconds even though permission is already correctly granted moments later. Previously (without this denial cache) each subsequent Check() would simply re-evaluate permissions and succeed as soon as the grant was committed.

Check() now performs a full permission re-fetch from DB whenever the cached permission map denies a specific resource

Previously, getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions checked permCache first and returned the cached scope map unconditionally (whether or not it granted the specific requested resource), so a single cached entry served unlimited Check() calls for any resource until TTL expiry. After this change, that internal cache check was removed from getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions; now, whenever getCachedIdentityPermissions finds a cached map but checkPermission against it returns false (resource not found in the cached scope map), Check() falls through and calls getIdentityPermissions again, which unconditionally re-queries permissionStore.GetUserPermissions from the DB. Only the new per-resource permDenialCache prevents repeating this for the exact same resource later. For workflows that call Check() once per resource across many distinct dashboards/folders a user cannot access, each first encounter with a new resource now triggers a full DB permission listing query instead of being resolved for free from the already-valid cached permission map, multiplying DB load compared to before.

Denial cache key uses unresolved subject id, inconsistent with other caches

userPermDenialCacheKey is built from checkReq.UserUID, which is the raw identifier parsed directly from the request subject (could be a numeric legacy ID or a UID depending on caller). All other per-user caches (idCache, permCache, teamCache, basicRoleCache) key on the canonical resolved UID obtained via GetUserIdentifiers. If the same user is referenced by different subject formats across calls (e.g. numeric ID in one call, UID in another), the denial cache entries will not be shared between them, reducing the cache's effectiveness and making its behavior inconsistent with the rest of the caching scheme.

permissionCacheUsage metric conflates two distinct caches and mislabels cache hits

The permissionCacheUsage metric is incremented with "true" both when the new permDenialCache short-circuits (line ~118) and when the permission cache actually grants access (line ~132), even though these are two separate caches with different semantics. Additionally, when getCachedIdentityPermissions returns a cached map but checkPermission determines the specific resource is not granted, the code unconditionally records permissionCacheUsage "false" (line 137) even though the permission cache was in fact consulted (just insufficient for this resource). This makes the metric unreliable for distinguishing actual cache-miss rates from 'cache hit but resource not covered' cases, undermining monitoring/alerting based on this metric.

No test exercises the write path of the new denial cache

TestService_CacheCheck's "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" test manually seeds s.permDenialCache and verifies that Check() reads it, but no test verifies that Check() actually populates permDenialCache after a genuine denial computed from the store (the new write at service.go's s.permDenialCache.Set call). The existing 'should deny user without permission' test in TestService_Check only checks the response value and never asserts that a subsequent call benefits from (or is affected by) the newly written denial cache entry, leaving this core new behavior without direct coverage.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

This PR fundamentally changes SQL expression behavior (TablesList/RunCommands/QueryFramesInto now always return "not implemented", and ReadQuery now always errors for QueryTypeSQL), but none of the changed files are tests. Given there must be pre-existing tests exercising pkg/expr/sql/parser.go (TablesList) and pkg/expr/sql_command.go (NewSQLCommand/Execute) that previously asserted correct DuckDB-based behavior (e.g. extracting table names, running real queries), those tests would now fail against the stubbed-out DB that always returns errors, since they are not included/updated in this diff. Conversely, no new test verifies that SQL expressions are now reliably blocked regardless of the FlagSqlExpressions toggle value (i.e., a regression test for the security fix itself is missing). For a PR whose entire purpose is to close an RCE/LFI vulnerability, lacking a test asserting the vulnerable path is unreachable is a significant gap that risks silent regression in future refactors.

Error message "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is misleading

When QueryTypeSQL is requested, ReadQuery now returns the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented". This is factually incorrect — SQL Expressions were implemented and are being deliberately disabled for security reasons (RCE/LFI, per CVE-2024-9264), not because the feature was never built. Users/administrators who previously had FlagSqlExpressions enabled and relied on it will see a confusing message implying the feature never existed, rather than a clear message indicating it has been disabled. This can misdirect support/debugging efforts and should be reworded (and ideally referenced in release notes/changelog, since this is a breaking change for anyone who had the toggle on).

Leftover "duckDB" variable name contradicts stated PR goal of removing DuckDB references

The PR description states the goal is to "Remove reference to DuckDB", yet the local variable in TablesList is still named `duckDB` (`duckDB := NewInMemoryDB()`) even though it now constructs the stub `sql.DB`, not a DuckDB instance. This is purely cosmetic but is inconsistent with the PR's own stated intent and could confuse future readers into thinking real DuckDB code still exists here.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing double-check of cache after acquiring write lock

After the first (read-locked) check of entryPointAssetsCache fails (e.g., cache not yet populated or cfg.Env == Dev), the code acquires the write lock at line 48 but never re-checks whether another goroutine already populated the cache while waiting for the lock. As a result, under concurrent initial requests (common right after startup), multiple goroutines can all proceed past the first check, serialize on the write lock, and each redundantly re-read and re-parse assets-manifest.json (or hit the CDN) even though the first goroutine already finished and stored a valid result. This doesn't reintroduce the data race, but it defeats part of the purpose of caching and wastes I/O/CPU under load. A standard fix is to re-check `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` immediately after acquiring the write lock and return early if so.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing second cache check after acquiring the write lock, which allows goroutines that passed the initial read-locked check to redundantly populate an already-filled cache.

false_positives.candidate:
No regression test added for the data race fix

The PR fixes a data race on the global entryPointAssetsCache variable in GetWebAssets, but no test was added (e.g., a test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently from multiple goroutines, intended to be run with `go test -race`) to guard against regressions. Without such a test, a future refactor could silently reintroduce the race with no automated signal.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Routine, successful batch cleanup progress logged at Error level with full ID list dumps

In `CleanAnnotations` (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` (lines 576, 579), every successful batch iteration logs via `r.log.Error(...)` even though no error occurred (the `err` field logged is always nil at that point, since the function already returned early on error).
