false_positives.candidate:
absolutize_urls mangles protocol-relative URLs

`absolutize_urls` treats any `href`/`src` starting with `/` as site-relative and rewrites it by stripping all leading slashes and prepending `prefix + "/"`. Protocol-relative URLs such as `//cdn.example.com/image.png` also start with `/`, so `href.sub(/^\/+/, '')` strips both leading slashes, turning the URL into `cdn.example.com/image.png`, which then becomes `prefix/cdn.example.com/image.png` (e.g. `http://eviltrout.com/cdn.example.com/image.png`) — a broken link to the wrong host instead of the intended absolute external resource. This affects both the `a['href']` and `img['src']` rewriting blocks (lines ~62-73).

raw_html cook method bypasses sanitization for externally-sourced content

`Post#cook` now returns `raw` verbatim (skipping `PrettyText`/`post_analyzer.cook`) when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. This mode is used for all posts created via `TopicEmbed.import` (app/models/topic_embed.rb line 22), including content pulled from `app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb`, which feeds raw RSS/Atom `content` (only `CGI.unescapeHTML`'d, never sanitized) directly into `TopicEmbed.import`. The resulting `cooked` value is later rendered unescaped via `<%= raw post.cooked %>` in app/views/embed/best.html.erb. If the configured feed (or a compromised/hijacked feed source) contains `<script>` or other malicious markup, it will be served verbatim to all visitors of the embed page, bypassing Discourse's normal HTML sanitization pipeline entirely — a stored XSS risk.

Race condition can raise unhandled uniqueness violation in TopicEmbed.import

When `embed.blank?` is true, a new Topic/Post/TopicEmbed is created. Two concurrent calls to `import` for the same new `embed_url` (e.g. two users hitting the embed controller at the same time before any embed exists) can both see `embed.blank? == true` and both attempt `TopicEmbed.create!(embed_url: url, ...)`. The unique index on `embed_url` (migration 20131217174004) will reject the second insert, but there is no rescue for `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique`/`StatementInvalid`, so the second caller's `TopicRetriever`/background job will raise an unhandled exception instead of gracefully reusing the already-created embed.

Disqus import tool silently drops the --category option

The previous implementation accepted `-c/--category` to assign imported Disqus threads to a specific category and passed `category: category_id` into `PostCreator.new`. The new implementation calls `TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], title: t[:title])`, which has no way to specify a category, and the `method_option :category` declaration itself was removed. Any existing script or documentation relying on `thor disqus:import -c <category>` will now silently ignore the option (or error, since the option no longer exists), a backward-incompatible regression with no migration note.

Test does not stub TopicView.new's return value

`TopicEmbed.expects(:topic_id_for_embed).returns(123)` and `TopicView.expects(:new).with(123, nil, {best: 5})` mock `TopicView.new` without a `.returns(...)`, so it returns `nil` by default. The controller then sets `@topic_view = nil` and implicitly renders `best.html.erb`, which calls `@topic_view.posts.present?` — this will raise `NoMethodError` on `nil`, so the subsequent `after` block assertion (`response.should be_success`) can never be reached; the test will error rather than pass/fail meaningfully, meaning the 'creates a topic view when a topic_id is found' path is not actually verified to render correctly.

Same cache duration applied to loading and completed states

`discourse_expires_in 1.minute` is called unconditionally for both the "loading" (topic not yet retrieved) and "found" (topic_view rendered) branches. If any HTTP cache/CDN sits in front of this response, the "loading" page can be cached for up to a minute, so the client-side `document.location.reload()` in `loading.html.erb` (which fires every 30s) may keep receiving the stale cached loading page even after the topic has actually been imported, delaying the user from seeing the real content.

feed_key is computed but never used

`feed_key` builds a Redis key intended to track feed modification state (likely for conditional GET / avoiding reprocessing unchanged feeds), but it is never referenced anywhere in `poll_feed` or elsewhere in the job. As written, every hourly poll fully fetches and parses the entire feed and calls `TopicEmbed.import` for every item regardless of whether the feed has changed, which is unnecessary load on the external feed source; the dead `feed_key` method suggests this optimization was intended but not wired up.

Unused translation key `embed.permalink`

The new `embed.permalink: "Permalink"` string is added to the locale file but is never referenced by any of the new embed views or controller (`app/views/embed/best.html.erb`, `app/views/embed/loading.html.erb`, `app/controllers/embed_controller.rb`), making it dead i18n content left over from an unfinished feature.

postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

Duplicate `self.downsize` definition silently discards the original 4-arg method

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side max upload size hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring configured site settings

`validateUploadedFile` previously read `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, honoring separate admin-configured limits for images (`max_image_size_kb`) and attachments (`max_attachment_size_kb`). It is now hardcoded to `10 * 1024` KB for both types. Attachments cannot be downsized server-side the way images can, so an admin who configured a smaller `max_attachment_size_kb` will no longer have that limit enforced client-side; uploads up to 10MB will be attempted and only fail (if at all) after the fact, producing a confusing UX and bypassing the admin's intended restriction. The same hardcoding is repeated for the 413 (entity too large) error message at line 246, which previously reported `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` and can now show an incorrect max size to users if the server's actual limit differs from 10MB.

false_positives.candidate:
Animated GIF detection never triggers because tempfile paths have no extension

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)` passes `tempfile.path` as the `from` argument. Inside `OptimizedImage.optimize`, the check `from =~ /\.GIF$/i` (optimized_image.rb line 155) decides whether to use the gifsicle-based animated instructions. Rack/ActionDispatch tempfiles typically have no file extension (e.g. `/tmp/RackMultipart...`), so this regex will never match for uploads coming through this new code path. As a result, large animated GIFs that need downsizing will always go through the regular ImageMagick `downsize_instructions`, which selects only the first frame (`#{from}[0]`), silently stripping the animation from any animated GIF that exceeds `max_image_size_kb`.

Downsizing loop ignores failure and may silently upload an oversized image

The loop at lines 64-70 calls `OptimizedImage.downsize` up to 5 times but never checks its boolean return value. `convert_with` (and therefore `downsize`) returns `false` on any ImageMagick/gifsicle failure (e.g. missing binary, malformed input, unsupported geometry string). If downsizing fails on every attempt, the loop exits solely because `attempt` reaches 0, and the code proceeds to call `Upload.create_for` with the original oversized `tempfile` and no error is surfaced to the caller or the user. This defeats the purpose of the size check and can let files larger than the configured `max_image_size_kb` through unnoticed.

No test coverage for the new automatic downsizing feature

The PR adds a new downsize-on-upload code path (lines 63-70) plus corresponding API changes in `optimized_image.rb` (collapsing `downsize` to a 3-arg/percent-based signature), but no tests were added or updated to cover: downsizing being triggered when `max_image_size_kb` is exceeded, the loop giving up after 5 attempts, or the behavior change to `OptimizedImage.downsize`'s signature. Given this changes both a public model API and upload behavior, the lack of tests makes it easy for the regressions noted above (duplicate method definition, lost GIF animation, silent oversized uploads) to go unnoticed before release.

The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate: Notification-level mutation performed as a side effect of a plain GET request, with no idempotency or CSRF protection The new `unsubscribe` action (routed via GET in config/routes.rb lines 440-441) mutates `TopicUser#notification_level` directly inside a GET request handler, with no confirmation step and no CSRF protection (GET requests are not covered by Rails' CSRF token checks). Because the action is keyed off the logged-in session (current_user) rather than a signed one-time token (unlike the existing key-based `email/unsubscribe/:key` route), any page that causes the user's browser to issue a GET to this URL while they are logged in (e.g. an tag, link prefetching, or an email security scanner following the link) can silently change their notification settings. Additionally, the mutation is not idempotent: every visit to the same URL re-evaluates `tu.notification_level > regular` using the *current* (already mutated) value, so repeated visits (page refresh, back/forward navigation, duplicate email link clicks, or automated re-fetching) progressively downgrade watching/tracking -> regular -> muted, fully muting the topic after just two visits even though the user only intended a single click.

Direct TopicUser save bypasses the canonical TopicUser.change path

The new action mutates `tu.notification_level` and calls `tu.save!` directly instead of using `TopicUser.change(current_user, topic_id, notification_level: ...)`, which is the method used everywhere else in the codebase (e.g. TopicsController#set_notifications) for this kind of update. This bypasses: setting `notifications_changed_at`/`notifications_reason_id`, publishing the `/topic/#{topic_id}` MessageBus event (so any other open tab/browser showing the topic will not reflect the new notification state in real time), and the `observe_after_save_callbacks_for` hook (e.g. UserActionObserver). This creates an inconsistent code path for notification-level changes and a real-time UI sync gap.

unsubscribe_link translation now silently requires an unsubscribe_url interpolation value

`config/locales/server.en.yml`'s `unsubscribe_link` key now contains `%{unsubscribe_url}`, which `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` (used in both `html_part` at line 67 and `body` at line 90) will try to interpolate. `template_args` only contains `:unsubscribe_url` if the caller of `build_email`/`MessageBuilder.new` passed it in `opts`. This means it searches the destinationCalendar array for an entry whose `externalId` equals the already-known falsy value, which will essentially never match a real calendar entry. As a result, `updateEvent` ends up calling the Google API with `calendarId: undefined` (likely causing API errors), and `deleteEvent` silently falls back to the hardcoded `"primary"` calendar instead of the correct host-specific calendar. This defeats the multi-host destinationCalendar support this PR is meant to add for update/delete flows whenever a booking reference lacks a stored externalCalendarId (e.g. legacy bookings or non-primary calendars).

updateEvent() never returns externalId/credentialId, dropping calendar reference tracking on location change

`EventResult` now has an `externalId` field and `EventManager.updateLocation()` builds `referencesToCreate` using `externalCalendarId: result.externalId` and `credentialId: result.credentialId ?? undefined` (previously it fell back to `evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId`/`?.credentialId`). However, `CalendarManager.updateEvent()`'s returned object (lines 313-322) never sets `externalId` or `credentialId` - only `createEvent()` does. Consequently, after a booking's location is edited (`updateLocation()`), the newly created booking reference will always have `externalCalendarId: undefined` and `credentialId: undefined`, losing the information needed to target the correct calendar for future updates/deletes of that booking, especially important for multi-host bookings where picking the wrong credential/calendar is now possible.

Organizer attendee email override uses the first destinationCalendar entry regardless of which host's credential is creating/updating the event

In both `createEvent` (lines 100-124) and `updateEvent` (lines 198-230), `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is simply the first entry of `event.destinationCalendar` (an array now containing every host's destination calendar). This value is used to override the organizer attendee's `email` field. Since `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents`/`updateAllCalendarEvents` invoke this service once per host/credential while passing the same shared `event` object (with the full array), every host's calendar-event creation/update will use the FIRST host's calendar externalId for the organizer attendee email instead of the calendar belonging to the credential actually performing the call (which is already correctly resolved via `selectedCalendar`/`credentialId` elsewhere in the same function). This can produce incorrect organizer attendee identities in secondary hosts' calendar events.

Team hosts' destination calendars silently dropped when evt.destinationCalendar resolves to null

`destinationCalendar` on `evt` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` exist. Later, `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is used to append other hosts' destination calendars for collective events. Because `evt.destinationCalendar` can be `null`, the optional chaining makes this push a no-op in that case, silently discarding all other hosts' destination calendars. This is precisely the scenario this PR is meant to fix (collective event with multiple hosts having calendars), so bookings where the organizer has no destination calendar but other hosts do will still fail to deliver calendar invites to those hosts.

Dropped organization.slug selection in rewritten loadUsers() for dynamic bookings

The rewritten `loadUsers()` function's dynamic-user-list branch (`!eventTypeId`) queries `prisma.user.findMany` with `select: { ...userSelect.select, credentials: true, metadata: true }`, but the previous implementation also selected `organization: { select: { slug: true } }`. This field is no longer fetched for dynamic bookings. If any downstream logic in this handler or in email/booking link generation for dynamic events relies on `user.organization.slug`, it will now be undefined, which is an unrelated regression introduced while refactoring this function for the destinationCalendar changes.

Calendar event creation for multiple hosts is now sequential instead of parallel

In `createAllCalendarEvents`, the new `for (const destination of event.destinationCalendar) { ... await createEvent(credential, event, destination.externalId) ... }` loop awaits each host's calendar event creation sequentially. For a collective event with N hosts, this results in N sequential network calls to external calendar providers instead of running them concurrently (as the credential-type branch below it still does via `Promise.all`). This can noticeably increase booking latency for collective events with several hosts that each have a calendar connected.

No new/updated tests cover the multi-host destinationCalendar array behavior

The PR converts `destinationCalendar` to an array across the whole booking/calendar pipeline (EventManager, CalendarManager, multiple calendar app services) but the only test change is updating one expected value from `null` to `[]` in an existing webhook e2e test. The PR description explicitly acknowledges no tests were added to prove the fix works. Given the number of subtle correctness issues identified in the array-handling logic (e.g. in GoogleCalendarService update/delete calendar resolution, and the dropped team destinationCalendar push), this feature lacks test coverage for the core multi-host invite scenario the PR claims to fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
forEach callback made async but not awaited, breaking error handling and ordering

The callback passed to `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(...)` was changed from a synchronous function to an `async` function so that `getCalendar` can be awaited inside it. However, `Array.prototype.forEach` never awaits the promises returned by its callback, so the surrounding `try { ... } catch (error) { logger.error(...) }` block (lines 124-139) no longer catches errors that occur inside the async callback (e.g. from `getCalendar` or `calendar.deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting`) — they become unhandled promise rejections instead. In addition, execution proceeds to the subsequent 'Send emails' step and the function's return without waiting for the calendar/video deletions to actually finish, so cancellations can race with (or occur after) the reschedule email being sent, and failures are silently swallowed instead of logged. Previously (sync callback + sync getCalendar) the try/catch correctly caught thrown errors synchronously. This should use `for (const bookingRef of bookingRefsFiltered)` with awaited iterations, or `Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => {...}))` awaited before continuing.

Since `forEach` does not await the returned promises, the enclosing try/catch (lines 124-139) can no longer catch errors thrown inside the callback, they become unhandled rejections. The function also proceeds to send the reschedule email and return before the calendar/video deletions have resolved, introducing a race condition where the booking is reported as rescheduled/cancelled while the actual calendar/video cleanup may not have completed or may fail without being logged.

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach((bookingRef) => {...})` was changed to `forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` to allow `await getCalendar(...)`. `Array.prototype.forEach` ignores the promises returned by async callbacks, so this code fires off calendar/video deletion calls without waiting for them. The mutation then immediately proceeds to call `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` and send webhooks (lines 570-618) without any guarantee that the previous calendar event/video meeting has actually been deleted/updated, and any thrown error inside the callback becomes an unhandled promise rejection rather than being surfaced to the caller. This should use a for...of loop or `Promise.all` with `.map` so the async work is properly awaited before continuing.

Dynamic import() calls execute eagerly at module load, not lazily on access

`appStore` is an object literal whose property values are `import("./X")` calls. These dynamic import expressions are evaluated immediately when the object literal itself is evaluated (i.e. as soon as this module is loaded), not when a specific key such as `appStore.googlecalendar` is actually accessed. As a result, every consumer that imports `appStore` (getCalendar, videoClient, payment handlers, etc.) still triggers loading of all ~27 app sub-packages concurrently on every module load, rather than only the app that is actually needed for a given credential/booking. This does not provide selective/lazy loading of individual apps — it only converts previously-synchronous property access into asynchronous access (via `await appStore[key]`) while still eagerly fetching every app module. This may fail to deliver the performance/bundle-size benefit implied by the PR, while adding `await` boilerplate throughout many call sites.

getCalendarCredentials now returns an unresolved Promise for `calendar`, risking silent breakage for other callers

`getCalendarCredentials` calls `getCalendar(credential)` (now async) without awaiting it, so the `calendar` field in its returned objects changed from a resolved `Calendar | null` value to an un-awaited `Promise<Calendar | null>`. Within this file, `getConnectedCalendars` was updated to `await item.calendar` correctly, but `getCalendarCredentials` is an exported utility and this PR's file list does not show every consumer of it being updated. Any other caller that destructures `calendar` and does a truthiness check (e.g. `if (calendar) {...}`) will now always treat it as truthy because a Promise object is always truthy, silently breaking null-handling logic for credentials whose calendar service failed to initialize. This contract change should be verified against all call sites of `getCalendarCredentials`, not just the one touched in this diff.

getVideoAdapters now resolves app lookups sequentially instead of in parallel

The previous implementation built the adapters array synchronously via `Array.reduce`. The new implementation uses a `for...of` loop with `await appStore[appName]` inside, resolving each credential's app module one at a time instead of concurrently (e.g. via `Promise.all`). For callers that pass multiple credentials (e.g. `getBusyVideoTimes`), this serializes N dynamic-import resolutions where they could be run in parallel, adding unnecessary latency proportional to the number of credentials.

No tests added for the new async appStore resolution / concurrency behavior

This PR converts many previously-synchronous app-store lookups (getCalendar, getVideoAdapters, payment app resolution) into asynchronous ones and changes several forEach loops to async callbacks. None of the changed files include test updates verifying that calendar/video deletions during booking cancellation/reschedule actually complete before the function returns, or that errors from the now-async app lookups are still surfaced/logged correctly. Given the concurrency regressions introduced by the `forEach(async ...)` pattern in this PR, a regression test exercising cancellation/reschedule with a failing or slow calendar/video provider would have caught the issue.
